PART ONE — THE WINDOW
Grease

The lanolin came out of the tub in a wad, the colour of old teeth, and it did not want to leave the tub. Dariush worked it between his palms for a full minute before it softened enough to spread, and even then it went on in ropes rather than in a film, and had to be pushed flat with the heel of the hand.
He started at the back of her neck.
"You're cold already," he said.
"I'm always cold. It's June."
"August."
"It's always June."

She was sitting on the third step down from the top of the harbour wall at Donaghadee, in a costume and nothing else, with her hair already under the first cap, and the granite was taking heat out of the backs of her thighs at a rate she could have quantified if she had wanted to. She did not want to. There were things it was useful to know and things it was useful to have stopped knowing, and after twenty-nine years in cold water the line between them had settled roughly where her skin was.

Dariush greased the trapezius first, both sides, then the deltoid heads, then the long muscle down the outside of the upper arm where the costume strap would sit for the next thirty hours and saw a groove if it was not attended to. He worked slowly. He had done this several hundred times and had never once done it quickly.
"Armpits," he said.
She lifted her arm.

The lanolin was cut fifty-fifty with zinc oxide, which was his own preference and not standard, and which he defended on the grounds that the zinc stayed put longer in salt water and had the additional benefit of being visible, so you could see what you had missed. Farangis had stopped arguing about it around 2009. The mixture smelled of sheep and of the inside of a chemist's. It smelled, more than anything else, of the four hours before a swim, which meant that it smelled of the top of the stomach going hollow, and she had long since stopped being able to separate the smell from the sensation. Pavlov had done his dogs with a bell. Twenty-nine years had done her with a tub of grease.
"Other one."
She lifted the other arm.

Out past the harbour mouth the water was doing the flat, oiled, unconvincing thing it did in a high-pressure system, the surface holding the light like a skin of milk, and the Copeland Islands sitting three miles off in a haze that would not decide whether it was haze or the beginning of a fog. Two men were fishing off the end of the south pier. A child was throwing bread at gulls that had long ago stopped needing it. Behind her the town went about the last Sunday in July with the particular Ulster listlessness of a seaside place that has been a seaside place for two hundred years and has run out of things to say about it.
"Neck again," said Dariush. "You'll turn to breathe eight thousand times before it gets dark."
"Forty thousand."
"Before it gets dark."
She said nothing. He greased the neck again.

There was a rule, and the rule was the only thing about the sport that had never once been ambiguous, and it went like this: from the moment the swimmer's body entered the water at the start, until the moment the swimmer cleared the water at the finish under her own power, no part of the swimmer might touch the boat, and no part of any other person might touch the swimmer. Not the pilot. Not the feeder. Not the observer. Not a doctor. Not a spouse. The swimmer could be spoken to. The swimmer could be shouted at, encouraged, insulted, sung to, prayed over. Food could be thrown to her or extended on a pole and released before she took it. But a hand laid on her shoulder for one second, even to steady her, even in kindness, even in an emergency, and the swim was over. Not disputed. Not appealed. Over.

Every sport has a rule that looks arbitrary from outside and turns out, when you have lived inside it long enough, to be the entire moral architecture of the thing. This was hers. The swim is only a swim if nobody helps you. And so the sport had constructed, with great care and over a hundred and fifty years, a situation in which four adults sat in a boat six feet from a person in visible distress, for thirty hours, and were forbidden to reach out.
Dariush was the last person permitted to touch her. He had about four minutes left.

He knew it, and she knew that he knew it, and neither of them had ever said so, because saying so would have made the greasing into a ceremony, and if the greasing became a ceremony then she would start to feel it, and if she started to feel it she would be no good at the thing she had to be good at, which was not feeling anything for a day and a half.
"How's the shoulder," he said.
"Fine."
"How is it actually."
"It's fine, Dariush. It's a shoulder. It hurts. It's supposed to hurt. If it stopped hurting I'd want to know why."
He pressed his thumb into the space under the acromion, hard, the way he had been shown by a physiotherapist in Bangor in 2004, and she made a small sound through her nose and did not otherwise move.
"That's fine," he agreed.

She stood up. The grease made her look like something that had been prepared rather than dressed, a bird, a joint, something with a temperature to be got to. He handed her the goggles. She spat in them, rubbed, rinsed them over the side, and put them on, and the world went the particular tea-brown of tinted polycarbonate, which she preferred to clear even at dusk, because clear lenses let you see how much of nothing there was.
"Two hours," she said. "Out to the fairway buoy, down along the shore, back."
"Water's twelve four."
"I know what the water is."
"I'm telling you anyway."
"I know."

She went down the steps. On the third from the bottom, where the weed started, she stopped, because she always stopped there, and turned, and he was standing at the top with the tub in one hand and his palms held out from his body, shining, useless.
"See you in a bit," she said.
"Yes."
She went in.

It is worth being precise about what happens to a body in twelve degrees of water, because the whole of what follows depends on it and because most people, including most doctors, are vague about it in a way that gets people killed.

The first thing is not the cold. The first thing is the gasp. Cold shock: a reflex, mediated by skin receptors, entirely involuntary, which produces an enormous inspiratory gasp followed by two to three minutes of uncontrollable hyperventilation, a tripling of respiratory rate, a spike in heart rate and blood pressure. It has nothing to do with fitness or will. It is the reason people drown thirty seconds after falling into water they could have swum across. If you gasp with your face under, you inhale water, and if you inhale water in twelve degrees your intercostals are already in spasm and you cannot cough it out.

Farangis did not gasp. She had not gasped since she was about fourteen. The response habituates — genuinely habituates, in the neurological sense, not the folk sense — after roughly six immersions, and stays habituated for a year or so, and can be maintained indefinitely by going in once a week, every week, in every month, for decades, which she had done. The gasp had been trained out of her the way a flinch is trained out of a boxer. What remained was a hard, bright, chemical clarity in the first thirty seconds, an alertness that no drug she had ever been offered came close to, and which was, she had privately concluded some time in her twenties, the actual reason she did this and not any of the reasons she gave in interviews.

The second thing is the hands. Peripheral vasoconstriction shuts down blood flow to the extremities to defend the core, which is sensible, and which costs you your fingers. Not immediately. Over hours. Grip goes first, then fine control, then the ability to close the hand at all, so that by hour twenty the fingers are splayed and the palm is a paddle and the catch at the front of the stroke, which is where all the propulsion comes from, is being made by a hand that no longer belongs to her in any sense she could defend philosophically.

The third thing is the core, and the core is the one that kills. Thirty-seven is normal. At thirty-five you are hypothermic and clumsy. At thirty-four your judgment is going and you will start making decisions that a person watching from six feet away can see are insane and that you will experience, from inside, as perfectly reasonable. At thirty-three you are in serious trouble. At thirty-two the shivering stops, which everyone misreads as improvement, and around here some people begin to feel warm, and take their clothes off, and lie down.

The fourth thing is that none of this is what stops swimmers. What stops swimmers is that at hour nine they are bored, and it is dark, and they cannot see their own hand, and they have eaten nothing but sugar for a day, and there is no reason on earth to continue.
She turned at the harbour mouth into the slight lop coming round the pier head, and put her face down, and began to count.

At the end of the two hours she came out at the slipway and Dariush was there with the flask and the towel and the two coats, and he did not touch her, because he had got out of the habit of touching her at the ends of swims, because for a decade the end of a swim had been the worst part of the day for both of them, and touch made it worse.
"Twelve two coming back," he said. "It dropped."
"I felt it drop."
"Wilson rang. He wants us at his house at eight."

She was shaking properly now, the deep shiver that comes on the beach and not in the water, the afterdrop, cold blood returning from the limbs to a core that had been managing without it. Her jaw was going. She got the coat round herself.
"Eight," she said.
"Eight."
"That's a window, then."
"He didn't say it was a window."
"He wouldn't say. But it's a window."

Dariush looked out at the flat brown water and the haze that had, in the two hours, decided it was fog after all, and had come in and taken the Copelands away entirely, so that there was nothing out there at all, no islands, no Scotland, no line where the sea stopped.
"Yes," he said. "It's a window."
The Window

Wilson's kitchen had a chart of the North Channel taped to the wall above the bread bin and had had one there, in one state of decay or another, since 1988. The current chart was six years old and had been annotated in four colours of biro by a man who did not believe in erasers. There were tide vectors on it. There were times. There were the names of people written next to smears of coastline, and about half of them had a date after the name, and about half of those had a line through the whole entry.
Farangis had learned, over three summers of coming to this kitchen, not to ask about the lines.
"Sit," said Wilson.
There were four chairs and there were five of them, so Ailbhe Nunan stood, which Farangis registered and filed and did not look at.

Wilson was sixty-five and had a face like a hand that had been left in water. He had piloted a hundred and forty attempts on the North Channel and had put fifty-one people onto the Scottish shore, which was the best ratio of any pilot working, and which he attributed entirely to being willing to tell people not to swim. He put a mug of tea in front of Farangis without asking whether she wanted one.

"Right," he said. "Neaps are Thursday. So your window, if you get one, is Wednesday night through Sunday morning, and after that the springs come in and the tide's running two and a half knots through the middle and you're not swimming that, nobody's swimming that."
"I know."
"I know you know. She doesn't." He nodded at nobody in particular, meaning the room, meaning the general condition of people. "Say it back to me anyway."
Farangis said it back to him. It was a ritual and she had learned not to resent it.

The North Channel is thirty-four and a half kilometres from Donaghadee to Portpatrick if you draw a straight line, and nobody has ever swum a straight line, and nobody ever will. The tide in the channel does not go up and down in any way that matters to a swimmer. It goes sideways. It comes north through the narrows on the flood at up to three knots in the middle, and it goes south on the ebb at about the same, and it changes its mind every six hours and twelve minutes, and a good swimmer moves at two and a half kilometres an hour, which is to say more slowly than the water she is in.
Which means the swim is not a swim. The swim is an arithmetic problem in which the swimmer is one term.

You leave on the last of one tide so that it carries you north into the channel. You are then swimming east across a river that is going north. Six hours later the river reverses and starts going south, and if you are not far enough across by then, it takes you back the way you came, and your track on the chart makes an S, and the S costs you six hours you do not have. Get it right and the two tides cancel and you cross in eleven, twelve, thirteen hours. Get it wrong and you are still swimming at hour twenty-two with Scotland four kilometres away and moving sideways past you like a train platform.
"So," said Wilson. "Wind."
He turned a laptop around. The forecast was a mess of colour.
"North-easterly Thursday, force four, gusting five. That's a no."
"Why," said Ailbhe, from the wall. It was the first thing she had said.

"Because a north-easterly runs against the flood and you get a short sea, a metre, metre and a half, close together, and she'll be breathing into it for six hours and she'll swallow half of it." He did not look up. "And because when it's like that I can't hold station without putting the boat on top of her, and if I put the boat on top of her that's her swim over and possibly her head."
"Right."

"Friday it backs westerly, force two, and that's lovely, and it's forecast to hold until it doesn't." He shut the laptop. "Which will be Saturday afternoon. So you're looking at a start somewhere in the small hours of Friday, and a finish before the wind comes in on Saturday, and that gives you about thirty hours of usable weather, and I have never in my life seen a forecast that far out be right."
"So we wait," said Farangis.
"So you wait."
"Until when."
"Until I ring you." Wilson took her mug away, which she had not finished, and put it in the sink, which meant the meeting was over.

"Two hours' notice. Maybe less. Don't go to Belfast. Don't drink. Don't get your hair cut, don't get a filling, don't eat anything you haven't eaten before, don't go near anybody with a child in a school, and don't, for the love of God, do anything on land that you can injure yourself with. I have lost more swims to people falling over on holiday than I have to weather."
They went out into the road. It was ten past nine and still light, that long Ulster August light that does not so much fade as get thinner, and the fog had come off the water and stood in the fields.
"Two days," said Dariush. "Maybe five."
"Maybe five."
"You'll go mad."
"Yes," said Farangis.

And here is the thing nobody puts in the documentaries. The swim is not the ordeal. The swim is the release. The ordeal is the four to six days beforehand in a rented room in a small town with a bag packed and a phone charged, tapering, which means not swimming, which means having in your body every single thing that swimming exists to remove, and nowhere to put it, and nothing to do but wait for a man in a bungalow to look at a chart and decide.
She had done it eleven times. She had, on four of those occasions, gone home without getting in the water at all.
"Farangis."
"What."
"She came," said Dariush.
"I saw."
"You asked her to come."
"I asked the association for an observer. She's the observer."
"Farangis."
"I asked for her," she said. "Yes."

They walked the rest of the way to the guesthouse without saying anything else, past the lifeboat station and the row of houses painted in the colours people paint houses when they can see the sea from them, and behind them the light went thin over the water, and somewhere out in it, thirty-four and a half kilometres away, the Scottish shore did what it had done for eleven summers, which was to sit there, entirely indifferent, being nineteen hours away.
The Hardest Water
There is a hierarchy and everybody in the sport knows it and nobody will write it down.

The English Channel is the original and will always be the one that matters to people outside the sport, because Webb did it in 1875 and because it is between two countries that write a great deal about themselves. Thirty-three kilometres, sixteen to eighteen degrees in August, the busiest shipping lane on earth, and about two and a half thousand successful crossings since the beginning. It is not easy. Nothing here is easy. But it has been made ordinary by volume: there is an industry at Dover, there are pilots with waiting lists three years long, and a fit person with two years of preparation and eight thousand pounds has a genuine chance.
The Catalina, off California, is twenty degrees and done at night for the flat water, and the difficulty is the distance and the dark.

The Molokai — the Kaiwi Channel, between Oahu and Molokai — is forty-two kilometres of open Pacific in twenty-five degrees, and the difficulty is that it is forty-two kilometres of open Pacific, with a swell that comes at you from three directions and things in it that are large.

The Tsugaru Strait in northern Japan is nineteen kilometres and a current that runs at four knots and will simply refuse you, over and over, for years, and where the successful crossings are decided almost entirely by the pilot.
Cook Strait. Gibraltar. The Sound between Denmark and Sweden. The Bristol Channel, which nobody outside these islands has heard of and which has a fourteen-metre tidal range and is genuinely lethal.
And then there is the North Channel, and everybody who has done more than four of these will tell you the same thing, which is that the North Channel is a different order of object.
Thirty-four and a half kilometres. Shorter than the Molokai. Barely longer than the English.
Eleven and a half to twelve and a half degrees.
Fewer than a hundred and thirty successful crossings in the whole history of the attempt.

Compare: two and a half thousand for the English. Nearly five hundred for Catalina. Over eight thousand people have stood on the summit of Everest. One hundred and twenty-six, at the last count Farangis had, had swum from Ireland to Scotland.
Three things do it, and they compound.

The first is the temperature. Twelve is not four degrees colder than sixteen in any sense that a body understands. Heat loss in water is driven by the gradient between the core and the medium, and the gradient at twelve degrees is a third larger than at sixteen, and the exposure is longer because you are slower, and the slowness is caused by the cold. It is not linear. The English Channel at sixteen degrees will take a well-insulated swimmer twelve hours and leave her at thirty-six degrees. The North Channel at twelve will take her thirty and put her at thirty-three, and everything that goes wrong in a marathon swim goes wrong below thirty-four.

The second is the tide. The North Channel is the neck of a funnel: the entire Irish Sea empties and fills through a gap forty kilometres wide, twice a day, and the water in the middle of it does not move like a tide, it moves like a river. Three knots on springs. A swimmer at two and a half kilometres an hour is doing about one and a third knots. The water is faster than the swimmer by a factor of two and there is nothing anybody can do about that except arithmetic.
The third is the jellyfish, and the jellyfish are the reason it is the North Channel and not simply a cold English Channel.

Farangis had a photograph on her phone that she had never shown anybody outside the sport, of a man she knew from Cork, taken four days after his successful crossing in 2019, and in it his back and shoulders were a solid raised lattice of purple lines from the base of the skull to the waist, hundreds of them, crossing and recrossing, and his face was so swollen on one side that his eye was closed.
He had finished. He is on the list. He would do it again.
And then, beneath the hierarchy of channels, there is the thing the hierarchy is actually for, which is the set.

The Oceans Seven. Somebody in the sport invented it in 2008 in conscious imitation of the Seven Summits, and the sport as a whole affected to find it vulgar and then, in the manner of every human institution that has ever been offered a list, organised itself around it entirely.
Seven channels. The English. The North. The Catalina. The Molokai. The Tsugaru. Cook Strait. Gibraltar.
Fewer than thirty people have completed all seven.
Farangis Roshanfar had six.

She had Gibraltar in 2010 and Catalina in 2012 and Molokai in 2013 and Cook in 2015. She had Tsugaru in 2018, at the fourth attempt, on a day when the current gave her forty minutes it had no reason to give her. She had the English Channel — a single, not the two-way — in 2008, when she was twenty-nine, in fourteen hours and nine minutes, with her husband on the boat and an eleven-year-old boy at home who had been told he could stay up.
She had six and she needed the North Channel.

And every profile that had ever been written about her, and there were four, and she had read them all twice, said the same sentence in some form: she is one of the Oceans Seven, one channel from the set.
It was not true and it had not been true since 2016.

She could not have explained it to a journalist in a way that would have survived editing. The list was a reason. The list was an excellent reason, a publicly legible reason, a reason that fitted in a caption, a reason that stopped people asking the actual question, which is the question everybody wants to ask a woman who lost her son in a channel and went on swimming channels.
The actual answer was that the North Channel is the coldest and longest of the seven, which means the deepest, which means the furthest in.
She wanted the last one because it was the worst one.
Habituation
To make a body that can survive twelve degrees for thirty hours you need three things, and only one of them is training.

The first is time in the water. Not fitness — time. Cold habituation is a real, measurable, physiological adaptation, and it is depressingly specific: it does not transfer from a cold shower, it does not transfer from an ice bath, it does not transfer from a sauna, and it does not transfer from last year. It comes from getting into cold water repeatedly and staying there, and it decays within a few weeks of stopping. There is no way to bank it. There is no way to shortcut it. There are people, mostly men, mostly on the internet, who believe otherwise, and Wilson had a folder of their emails.

So: two winters. Ballyholme Bay, six-fifteen in the morning, November through March, when the water goes from thirteen down to seven and a half and back up again. Six-fifteen because Dariush left for the Ulster at seven and because it is easier to do a difficult thing before you are properly awake. In November you can stay in for an hour. In February you can stay in for eighteen minutes, and if you stay in for twenty-five you cannot get your own coat on afterwards, which is a fact she had learned experimentally and which had frightened her badly enough that she now carried a second person with her in the form of an old woman named Sadie who swam in a bobble hat and shouted at her when she stayed too long.

The adaptations are these. Cold shock blunts — the gasp reflex goes quiet, the hyperventilation shortens from three minutes to about forty seconds. That is habituation, and it is the one that keeps you alive. Then there is a metabolic adaptation: brown adipose tissue, which everyone is told they lose in infancy and which cold-exposed adults quietly retain and can even regrow, generating heat directly without shivering. Non-shivering thermogenesis. It is not much. It is a few watts. In a body sitting at the edge of its thermal balance for thirty hours, a few watts is the difference between finishing and being lifted out.
And then there is the insulative adaptation, which is the one nobody wants to talk about, and which is: you get fatter.
Not fat. Fatter. There is a difference and the difference is the whole of a woman's relationship with the sport.

Subcutaneous fat is the only insulation permitted under the rules. No wetsuit. No neoprene of any kind. One standard costume, sleeveless, legless, one cap, one pair of goggles, grease. That is the list, and it has been the list since Webb crossed the English Channel in 1875, and the sport defends it with a ferocity that outsiders find either admirable or deranged depending on temperament. Which means the swimmer's insulation is her own body, and the amount of it she carries is not vanity in reverse but load-bearing engineering.

Farangis was five foot seven and had raced at nine stone four when she was twenty-two, in pools, in chlorine, in a country where the water was heated to twenty-seven and a half. She now weighed eleven stone nine. She had put on the last stone deliberately over fourteen months, by eating four hundred calories a day more than she wanted, most of it in the evening, most of it fat rather than sugar because sugar went straight to training. It was not enjoyable. Nobody understood this. She had been congratulated, in supermarkets, by women she barely knew, for having "let herself go a bit" and looking "well on it."
She had also been asked, on local radio, by a man in his thirties, whether she worried about what the training did to her figure.
She had said, "It's not a figure, it's a system."
He had laughed, because he thought she was being funny.

The truth was less quotable and worse. She had grown up in two countries that both, in entirely different registers and for entirely opposed reasons, had opinions about the size and visibility of a woman's body, and had spent thirty years arriving at a private, unshareable, faintly obscene delight in having found a discipline in which the correct answer was more. More flesh. More of her. A body that took up room in the world and was rewarded for it. When she stood on a scale at eleven stone nine and the needle went where she wanted it, she felt something she had no clean word for, and which was closer to lust than to satisfaction, and which she had never told anybody, including Dariush, including the sports psychologist in 2013, because it sounded — she had run the sentence many times in her head — it sounded like a woman enjoying her own destruction.
Because that is the other half of it. The fat is armour and the fat is also the thing that will be measured, at the end, by a coroner, if there is a coroner.

Her feet had been numb since 2019. Not during swims. Permanently. A band across the ball of the left foot and the outer two toes of the right, where the sensation had simply not come back one spring, and had not come back the spring after that. She had not seen anyone about it. She lived with an anaesthetist. She was aware of the irony, which was not really irony but cowardice, and she had a policy on it, which was: after.
There was a great deal filed under after.
Who Does This

The guesthouse on the New Road took swimmers because the woman who ran it, Marguerite, had a son who had swum the Channel in 2011 and had not stopped talking about it since, and because swimmers pay for a week and stay for two and eat almost nothing. In the last week of July there were four of them in the house, plus assorted crew, all waiting on the same neap tide and the same forecast and the same phone call from the same man.
It is worth looking at them, because people ask what kind of person does this, and the answer is not what they expect.

There was Colm, forty-four, an accountant from Sligo, on his fourth attempt at the North Channel. He had been pulled at nine hours, at fourteen hours, and — the one that had done something to him — at twenty hours and forty minutes, three and a half kilometres out, when the tide turned and Wilson's predecessor had made the call and Colm had argued with him from the water for eleven minutes before getting in the boat. He had a laminated printout of that track on his phone and would show it to anyone. He had spent, by his own estimate, thirty-one thousand pounds on the North Channel. He had two daughters, and the elder one had asked him at Christmas, apparently without malice, whether he would still be doing this when she was at university.

There was Nikki, twenty-four, from Perth, who had a sponsor and a drone and a following, and who filmed her feeds, and whose people had asked Marguerite whether the guesthouse could be described as a "base camp." Everybody had decided in advance to find her ridiculous and everybody had revised within two days, because she swam eight hours in twelve-degree water on the Tuesday without a single complaint and got out and ate a bowl of soup and went to bed at eight, and because when Colm's hands were too clawed to do up his own bag on the Thursday she did it for him without being asked and without saying anything about it, and because the ones with the sponsors are frequently the ones who have arranged their entire lives around a single thing and are therefore the most serious people in the room.

There was Anders, sixty-one, Danish, a widower of four years, who was attempting the channel because his wife had wanted him to stop doing it and he had stopped, for eleven years, and now there was no longer anyone to stop for. He said this on the second evening, cheerfully, over dinner, and nobody knew what to do with it, and Nikki asked him what her name had been, which was the correct question and which none of the rest of them had thought to ask.
And there was Farangis, forty-seven, who was there for the ratification of nothing.
So: what kind of person.

The sport selects, first, for tolerance of tedium. This is underrated to the point of being invisible. There is no scenery. There is no crowd. There is no ball, no opponent, no score, and for most of the swim there is no visual information of any kind other than a brown-green nothing, your own arm entering the water, and — if you are lucky — the hull of a boat. The stroke does not vary. The breathing does not vary. Thirty hours at sixty strokes a minute is one hundred and eight thousand identical movements. Anyone who requires stimulation is filtered out in the first year.

It selects, second, for a very particular relationship with pain, which is not the ability to endure it but the ability to be uninterested in it. Farangis had made this distinction to a journalist once and had watched it fail to land. Endurance implies a struggle: the pain arrives, you resist it, you win. That is not what happens. What happens, in the good hours, is that the shoulder hurts and the hurting is simply a fact about the environment, like the temperature, like the swell, and it does not have any particular claim on the attention. The pain is not defeated. It is demoted.
It selects, third — and this is the one that gets left out of the profiles — for people who are trying not to be somewhere.

Not all of them. Nikki, as far as anyone could tell, was in it for the perfectly clean reason that she was extremely good at it. But go round a table of open-water swimmers at eleven o'clock at night and you will find a divorce, a bereavement, a bottle put down eight years ago, a childhood nobody wants to describe, a job that eats the person doing it. The water is six hours a day in which nobody can ring you, nobody can ask you anything, and you are legally and physically unreachable. There is no other activity available to an adult with responsibilities that provides this. Meditation retreats attempt it and fail, because you can leave. You cannot leave the middle of the North Channel.
Colm said, on the Wednesday, drunk on one glass of wine because he had not had a drink in five months: "It's the only time nobody wants anything off me."
Anders said: "It is the only time I am not being brave."
Nikki said: "It's the only time I'm not on my phone," and everyone laughed, and she said, "No, I'm serious, that's the actual reason," and after a moment everyone stopped laughing.
Farangis said nothing, and refilled the water jug, and went up at half nine.

She lay in the dark in a rented room with her bag packed at the foot of the bed and listened to the fog signal on the Copelands going every sixty seconds, and did the thing she did every night, which was to run the first hour of the swim in her head, stroke by stroke, from the harbour steps to the fairway buoy, in real time, for as long as she could hold it before sleep took her.
She got about eleven minutes in.
It was further than usual.
Farangis at Nine

Karaj, 1988. A walled garden on the north side of the city with a rectangular pool in it that had been built for a family who no longer lived there, and which the current occupants had inherited along with the vine and the dead fountain and a caretaker named Hushang who was ninety per cent deaf and had views about the vine.

The pool was fourteen metres long. It was filled from a tank on the roof of the outbuilding and the water arrived at the temperature of the night before, which in March was about nine degrees and in August about twenty-two. There was no filter. Once a fortnight two men came and emptied it and scrubbed it and refilled it, and for the two days after that the water was clear and after that it was green.
Zohreh woke her daughter at twenty past five.

This is the memory Farangis kept, and she kept it whole, unlike almost everything else from those years, which had gone the way of a country's worth of childhoods and become a set of smells: her mother in a cotton housecoat with a towel over her arm, standing in the doorway of a bedroom, saying nothing at all, because the arrangement was that nothing was said. If Farangis got up, they swam. If she did not get up, her mother went back to bed and it was never mentioned. There was no compulsion in it anywhere. There was only the doorway, and the towel, and a nine-year-old deciding, in the dark, four or five mornings a week for six years, to put her feet on the floor.

They went out through the kitchen and across the grass, which was wet, and Zohreh took off the housecoat and folded it on the tiles and got in without a sound, sliding in at the shallow end and going under and coming up already swimming.
Her mother had been, between 1966 and 1971, one of the four fastest women in Iran over two hundred metres freestyle.

Farangis knew this the way children know things, which is to say she knew it as a piece of furniture rather than as information. There was a photograph in a drawer, not on a wall: eight girls in dark costumes on a tiled deck in Tehran, hair under white caps, and the third from the left had her mother's chin. There were no medals in the house. There was no swimming on the television and no club and no coach and no times, and when Farangis, at eleven, asked what her mother's best two hundred had been, Zohreh said, "It was a different pool," and got up to see to something on the stove, and that was the end of it.

What Farangis learned in that pool was not technique, although she learned technique, because her mother had the stroke of someone who had been taught properly by someone who had themselves been taught properly, and it transmitted. What she learned was the register.

They swam for fifty minutes and they did not speak. Not because speaking was forbidden — because it did not occur. The water at that hour was the temperature of the air at that hour and both were cold, and the sky went from black to grey to a hard white over the wall, and the two of them went up and down a fourteen-metre rectangle passing each other on the left, and the sound was breathing and hands going in.
Then, at ten past six, Zohreh would stop at the shallow end and stand with the water at her collarbones and look at the top of the wall.

Always the same. Fifteen, twenty seconds. Head back a little. Looking at the top of a garden wall in the north of Karaj with an expression that her daughter, at nine, read as tiredness, and at fourteen read as sadness, and at thirty-one, standing on a beach in County Down after her first Channel qualifier with her hands shaking too much to hold the flask, understood in one go, completely, and had to sit down on the shingle.
Her mother had been checking that the wall was still high enough.

That was all. That was the whole of it. She swam in a walled garden at dawn because it was walled and because it was dawn, in a decade when a woman of thirty-six who had raced in front of crowds in a dark costume in 1969 now swam where nobody could see her, and had made, without ever once saying so, an arrangement with the world: I will keep this, and I will keep it small, and I will keep it out of sight, and in exchange I will be allowed to keep it.

And she had passed it on. Not the arrangement — she was too careful for that. She had passed on the thing underneath the arrangement, which was that water is where you go to be unwitnessed, and that the pleasure of it is the pleasure of a room nobody can come into.

There is a straight line, and Farangis could draw it, from a woman in a cotton housecoat standing in a doorway at twenty past five to a woman of forty-seven who had arranged her entire life around the only sport on earth in which four people watch you for thirty hours and none of them is allowed to touch you.

She had never mentioned the line to a psychologist. She had mentioned a version of it to Dariush, once, in 2011, three weeks after Zohreh died, in a car park in Dundonald, and he had listened for a long time and then said the wrong thing, which was: "So it's her fault."
And she had said, "No. It's her gift."
And he had said, "Farangis, those are the same sentence."
The First Cold

They came to Northern Ireland in the spring of 1990 for reasons that were entirely legible on a form and entirely unspeakable in the house. Her father had a brother in Belfast who had come in 1974 to do a doctorate and had stayed. There was a job. There was a semi-detached in a street off the Bangor Road with a garage that never held a car. There was a school where the register went Anderson, Bell, Crawford, Dunlop, and then stopped, visibly, for a beat, before the teacher attempted her surname.

She was eleven. She learned English in fourteen months in the way children do, completely and without accent and at the cost of losing the ability to read Persian at any speed, which she would regret for the rest of her life.
What is relevant here is not the migration. What is relevant is the register the household kept afterwards.

Her father had been a hydrologist. In Belfast he did a job that involved water in a way that could be described at a dinner table without anyone having to look at their plate, and he did it for twenty-two years, and he was good at it, and he never once complained about it, out loud, in her hearing, in her life.
Her mother swam in the sea now, because there were no walls in County Down and it turned out there did not have to be, and she never once said anything about that either.
There was food in the house. There was heat in the house. There was, on the wall of the front room, a framed print of a bridge in Isfahan that nobody looked at.

And there was a rule, which was never stated, and which every child of that kind of household will recognise instantly: the family's allowance of grievance had already been spent. Not by anyone in particular and not on anything you could point to. It had simply been used up, somewhere between one country and another, and what remained was a fixed quantity of complaint per household per year, and it was gone, and if you needed some you were out of luck.

So you did not say you were cold. Not because you would be punished. Because there was nowhere to put it. Because the words I'm cold would arrive in a room where two adults were not saying substantially larger things, and would sit there being small.
This is the origin of it, and it is important that it is not heroic.

People assume that endurance athletes are built by hardship, and they picture something with shouting in it. The actual mechanism is quieter and more permanent. You are not taught to endure. You are taught that the readout is unavailable. The child learns to run a body without a dashboard, and the adult it becomes is not braver than other adults, she is simply missing an instrument that other adults use to make decisions.
Farangis got into the Irish Sea for the first time in November 1990, at Ballyholme, aged eleven, on a dare from a girl called Judith Herron who did not get in herself.

It was nine degrees. She had never been in nine degrees. She went to her waist and the cold shock hit and she made a noise she had never made and could not stop making, a kind of shrieking in-breath, over and over, and Judith Herron laughed on the beach in a duffel coat, and Farangis, unable to speak, unable to control her own diaphragm, and absolutely certain that this was the moment at which she would either become someone in this town or not, put her face in the water and swam twenty-five metres out and twenty-five metres back.
She came out. She could not do her own buttons. Her lips had gone a colour that Judith Herron stopped laughing at.

And she said — this is the part she never told anyone, not Dariush, not anyone, because she could not make it sound like anything other than a boast, and because it was not a boast, it was a diagnosis —
She said: "That's not cold."

She meant it. That is the terrible part. Standing on a beach in November with her core down a full degree and her hands finished, she genuinely, sincerely, from inside, believed that what she had just experienced did not qualify.
The instrument was not broken. It had never been fitted.

Judith Herron told everyone at school, and the story went round in the shape of a joke, and by Christmas Farangis was the girl who swam in the sea in winter, which was better than being the girl whose name the teacher stopped for, and she understood the exchange rate perfectly and paid it without hesitation, and has been paying it ever since.
The Year
The build for a North Channel takes twelve months and it is almost entirely boring, and the boredom is not incidental to it, the boredom is the training.

September to November. Base. Forty to fifty kilometres a week, six days, mostly in the sea while the sea is still fourteen degrees and habitable. Two sessions a day on Tuesdays and Thursdays: an hour before work at Ballyholme, two and a half hours in the evening at Groomsport or off the pier at Donaghadee if the wind was in the south-west. Long swim on Sunday, four hours minimum, building to six by November.

Nothing fast. This is the thing pool swimmers cannot make themselves believe: there is no speed work in a marathon build, none, not one session, because the event is contested at about sixty-five per cent of maximum heart rate and every minute spent above that is a minute spent training an energy system that will not be present after hour three.

Sixty-five per cent for six hours is a strange place to live. It is not hard. That is what nobody understands. At no point in a marathon swim, and at no point in training for one, is a swimmer out of breath. The event does not hurt in the way that a four-hundred hurts. It hurts the way a long march hurts: cumulatively, in the joints, in the same four muscles, over a duration that exceeds the mind's ability to hold an intention.

December to February. Cold maintenance, which is the least productive and most necessary phase. Volume drops to twenty-five kilometres because the sea is eight degrees and she cannot stay in it long enough to do more. Three sea swims a week of twenty to forty minutes, purely to keep the habituation alive. The rest in the pool at Bangor at twenty-eight degrees, which she hated with a completeness that had not diminished in thirty years.

Six-fifteen at Ballyholme, in the dark, in January. Sadie in the bobble hat with a stopwatch and a flask. Twenty minutes. Out. Coat, hat, sit in the car with the heater off for the first ten minutes because putting a cold body next to a heater is how you make the afterdrop worse.

The two of them sat in a Vauxhall in a car park in the dark four days a week for three months a year for eleven years and talked about, in strict order of frequency: the water temperature, the wind, Sadie's hip, a woman called Ann who had said something in 2019, and — twice, in eleven years, and only after the second of them — Sohrab.

March to May. Rebuild. Volume back to fifty, then sixty. The sea comes up through nine, ten, eleven. Sunday swims out to five hours, then six. She began doing them without a support boat, along the coast between Donaghadee and Ballywalter and back, which is not permitted for a qualifier but is what everybody does, and which meant that between the middle of April and the end of May there were four Sundays on which Farangis Roshanfar was alone in the Irish Sea for six hours with nobody within eight hundred metres of her.
Dariush knew. They had an arrangement about it which consisted of him not saying anything and her being back by two.

June to July. The specific phase. Volume peaks at seventy kilometres in the third week of June, which is twenty-two hours in the water, and everything else in the life is subordinate. She had reduced her hours at the school office in March. They had not been on a holiday since 2015.

The qualifier: six hours continuous in water below sixteen degrees, observed, which she had done at Strangford on a Saturday in June in twelve point nine, and which had been logged and countersigned and sent to the association, and which was the last piece of administration.

The night swims. Four of them, in the last five weeks, from ten at night until four in the morning, with Dariush in a kayak, along the shore, because the crossing would have nineteen hours of dark in it and a swimmer who has never swum through the small hours will discover at two in the morning that the dark is not the same darkness she was in at midnight.

The three-thirty swim, once, in the second week of July: six hours starting at half three in the morning, deliberately after four hours' sleep, deliberately underfed, to find out what her stroke did when the whole system was wrong.

Her stroke rate fell eleven per cent and her temper went completely and she called Dariush something in the water at half six in the morning that she apologised for in the car and that he told her, correctly, was extremely useful information.
And the food.

Fourteen months of eating four hundred calories a day more than she wanted. Full-fat everything. Cheese at eleven o'clock at night. A specific and now permanent revulsion for a particular brand of chocolate mousse that she had eaten every evening for six weeks in 2024 and could no longer look at in a supermarket.

She had gained fourteen pounds by January and another five by June and had held eleven stone nine from the last week of June, which was the target, and which was, according to a set of callipers and a spreadsheet, about twenty-eight per cent body fat, which is roughly what a healthy woman of forty-seven ought to have and which in her case had been assembled deliberately, item by item, like a wall.
Total for the twelve months: two thousand two hundred and eighty kilometres.

That is the answer to the question people ask, which is how do you train for something like that, and it is not an interesting answer, and the reason it is not interesting is the whole point. There is no secret. There is no method. There is a woman getting into cold water six days a week for a year and doing the identical movement eight million times, and the only genuinely difficult part of it, the part that removes ninety-nine people in a hundred, is the absolute unrelenting sameness of it in a life that has other things in it.
Dariush had said it once, at a dinner, to a surgeon who had asked, and Farangis had not known he had it in him:
"It isn't a sport. It's a devotion. There's a difference and the difference is that nobody is watching and there's no ball."
Feeds
On the Tuesday she made forty-one feeds in Marguerite's kitchen.
This is the least discussed and most decisive part of the entire discipline. Everyone thinks the swim is won by shoulders. The swim is won by the stomach, and the stomach is a coward.

The arithmetic. A swimmer of Farangis's size and speed burns somewhere between six and eight hundred kilocalories an hour in twelve-degree water, and the water figure is the reason the number is so brutal — a substantial share of it is going to thermoregulation, to simply not dying, and none of that share does anything to move her forward. Total muscle glycogen at the start is about two thousand kilocalories. So by hour three she is running on what she drinks, and she will do that for another twenty-seven hours.

You cannot make up the deficit. Nobody has ever made up the deficit. The upper limit on carbohydrate absorption in an exercising human gut is around sixty grams an hour for glucose alone, and can be pushed to about ninety by combining glucose and fructose, which use different intestinal transporters, and past that the sugar sits in the small intestine drawing water into the lumen and you get osmotic diarrhoea in the North Channel at four in the morning, which has happened, to people she knows, and which they do not talk about, and which is exactly as bad as it sounds because there is nowhere to go and nothing to do and you are not permitted to touch the boat.
So the target is eighty grams an hour and the tolerance for error is about ten either way.

She used maltodextrin, which is a glucose polymer with low osmolality, so you can get a lot of carbohydrate into a small volume without turning the drink into syrup; she cut it one part in four with fructose; she made it up at fifty grams per two hundred and fifty millilitres; and she added sodium, six hundred milligrams a litre, because thirty hours of sweating into salt water while drinking hypotonic fluid is the exact recipe for exercise-associated hyponatraemia, which does not feel like anything until it feels like a seizure.
Two feeds an hour. Every thirty minutes, on the half hour, from hour one to the end.

Warm. Not hot — hot is vomit at hour eighteen — warm, forty degrees going into the flask, which after two hours in a flask in a boat in a channel is about body temperature going down, and body temperature going down is the single most important comfort available to a person who has been in twelve degrees for a day, and the swimmers who have never done it do not believe this and the swimmers who have done it will tell you, without embarrassment, that they have wept at a feed.

Every fourth feed she took paracetamol. Every sixth, from hour twelve, a caffeine tablet, a hundred milligrams. From hour eighteen, if it was going badly, another. She had a protocol and the protocol was written on a laminated card that lived in Dariush's jacket, and it had his handwriting on it, and it was seven years old, and there was a line ruled through one item on it that neither of them had ever discussed.
The delivery. This is where the rule bites.

The feed goes into a bottle. The bottle is attached to a line, or to a pole, and the feeder extends it and lets go. The swimmer takes it, drinks, and releases it, and the feeder pulls it in. At no point may the line be taut while she holds it, because a taut line is assistance, and assistance is a tow, and a tow is the end of the swim. At no point may the feeder's hand come within reach.
Forty seconds. That is what a good feed costs. Thirty hours of swimming, sixty feeds, forty minutes of treading water in total, during which she is not moving forward and the tide is.

She lined the bottles up on Marguerite's counter, forty-one of them, and mixed each one and capped it and wrote the number on the lid in permanent marker, and Dariush sat at the table behind her with the crossword he had not filled in and watched her do it and did not offer to help, because it was hers.
At feed nineteen she stopped for a moment with the marker in her hand.
"What," he said.
"Nothing."
She wrote nineteen on the lid.

At the English Channel, ten years ago, the two-way, she had gone into the water at eleven at night, and she had turned at the French shore at hour eleven and forty minutes, and Sohrab had gone in at hour twelve as pace swimmer for the return leg, permitted, one hour in every three, no contact, and it had been feed nineteen when she last saw his arm going in beside hers.
She had never once, in ten years, been able to make herself write that number without stopping.
Outside a car pulled into the gravel and did not switch its engine off for a while.
"That'll be her," said Dariush.
The Observer

Ailbhe Nunan had been ratifying swims for twenty-six years and had the specific patience of someone whose entire professional function is to be present and to record and to have no opinion. She was fifty-eight, from Sligo, and she had a canvas bag with a clipboard in it and a thermometer and a watch and a copy of the rules that she had not needed to consult since about 2004.
She came into Marguerite's kitchen and put the bag on a chair and said, "Farangis."
"Ailbhe."
"You've made your feeds."
"I've made my feeds."
"Right." She looked at the counter, at the forty-one bottles with the numbers on the lids. "You always were tidy."

There are perhaps two hundred people in the world who do this job at this level. They are not officials in the sense that a referee is an official. Nobody is competing. There is no prize. The observer exists for one reason: because a marathon swim is unverifiable. Nobody sees it. There is no track, no timing gate, no camera that can watch a person for thirty hours in the dark. Everything that is known about what happened in the middle of a channel at three in the morning is known because one person in a boat wrote it down.

The observer records the start time and the finish time. She records water temperature and air temperature at intervals. She records stroke rate. She records every feed and its duration. She records the swimmer's condition in whatever language she chooses, which is where it becomes an act of composition rather than measurement. She records any contact, and if there is contact she records the swim as terminated, and there is no appeal, because there is nobody to appeal to.
And then she signs it. And then the swimmer signs it. And then it goes to the association, and the association ratifies, and a name goes on a list that fewer than a hundred and twenty people are on.
If the observer does not sign, nothing happened.
If the swimmer does not sign, nothing happened.
The whole edifice — the sport, the record, the hundred and fifty years of it — rests on two signatures in a boat.
"You know the wind's wrong until Friday," Ailbhe said.
"Wilson told us."
"I'll stay in the town. There's a place on the front does a room." She sat down without being asked, which was the first informal thing she had done. "Dariush."
"Ailbhe."
"You look well."
"I don't," said Dariush, "but thank you."
Marguerite came in and went out again, sensing something, the way people who run guesthouses sense things.
Ailbhe took the clipboard out of the bag and put it on the table, face down, which was either nothing at all or was the single most deliberate thing anyone had done in that room in a week.
"I was surprised to get the call," she said.
"There aren't many of you."

"There are nine of us who'll do a North Channel." She let it sit. "You asked for me by name, Farangis. Áine rang me and said, she's asked for you, and I said, right, and Áine said, do you want me to send someone else, and I said no."
"Why not."
"Because you asked for me by name."
The three of them sat in a guesthouse kitchen in Donaghadee with forty-one bottles of maltodextrin on the counter behind them and did not say the thing.

It had been ten years and two months. Ailbhe had been the junior observer on that boat, twenty-nine years into a career, on a two-way English Channel attempt in September, and she had written the log, and the log had been ratified, and the swim had been recorded as abandoned at hour twelve on the return leg. Cause: medical emergency on board. Two lines. She had chosen the words. She had had eleven hours in a boat coming back to Dover to choose them.
Farangis had never read it.

This is not a figure of speech. The document existed; a copy had come in the post in October 2016, in an envelope with the association's crest on it, and Dariush had opened it and read it and had then, without saying anything, put it in the drawer of the desk in the back bedroom under the fuse box instructions and the manual for a dishwasher they no longer owned, and it had been there ever since. Farangis knew exactly which drawer. She had stood in front of it, by her own count, four times.
"Ailbhe," she said.
"Mm."
"When it's over. When I get out. Before I sign anything."
Ailbhe Nunan looked at her for a moment with the perfect neutrality of a woman who has spent twenty-six years training herself not to have a face.
"Ask me in Portpatrick," she said.
"That's not a no."

"It's not a yes either." She stood up and picked up the bag and left the clipboard where it was, face down on the table, which meant she was coming back. "Get some sleep. He'll ring you at three in the morning one of these days and you'll want to have banked it."
She went out. The car started. It sat there again with the engine running for a while before it moved.
Dariush turned the clipboard over.
It was blank. A fresh log sheet, dated, with her name at the top spelled correctly, and every field after that empty.
Dariush
He had married a woman who left.

Not in the way people mean. She came back. She had always come back. In twenty-five years of marriage she had come back from Dover and Sanday and Lough Erne and Loch Lomond and Cork Harbour and the Bristol Channel and Robben Island and the Kaiwi Channel and a lake in Zurich and a fjord in Denmark, and she had come back from all of them, every single time, and had walked into the kitchen carrying a bag that smelled of a wet costume and had put the kettle on.

But she left. That was the shape of the marriage. He had understood it early — earlier than she had, he thought — that the person he had fallen in love with in a corridor at Queen's in 1996 was organised around an absence, and that the absence was not a wound in her but an appetite, and that the appetite was going to be fed at intervals for as long as her shoulders held out, and that his choice was to be the man who fed it or the man who did not.
He had been twenty-two. He had thought, with the total confidence of twenty-two, that he could be the man who fed it and also, eventually, the thing that replaced it.
He had been wrong about the second part and it had taken him about eleven years to be sure.

Dariush Roshanfar was a consultant anaesthetist. He had done the job for twenty-one years and he was, by any measure that mattered, extremely good at it, and the reason he was good at it was the reason that made the rest of his life impossible.

An anaesthetist knows numbers. That is the whole discipline: you take a human being to the edge of a set of physiological cliffs and you hold them there for four hours and you know, at every second, exactly how far the edge is. He could tell you what a core temperature of thirty-four does to the coagulation cascade. He could tell you the mechanism by which cold diuresis strips a swimmer's plasma volume and why that makes the afterdrop worse. He could tell you, because he had looked it up in 2003 when he first understood what she was going to do with her life, the survival curves for immersion in twelve degrees, and the specific point on the curve at which rescue stops being a rescue and becomes a recovery.
And then he stood on a harbour wall and greased the shoulders of the woman he loved and watched her walk into it.
Forty times a year. Every year.

People asked him how he coped and he had a line for it, which was: "She's very good at it." It landed. It ended the conversation. It was even true. It was also the most complete lie he told, because coping was not what he did. What he did was more like the thing you do with an untreatable diagnosis: he had made an arrangement in which the knowledge lived in a specific room, and he did not go into that room, and the not-going-in was a full-time occupation that he had been performing for a quarter of a century and that nobody had ever seen him do.
Here is what he actually did during her swims.

He fed her. He counted her stroke rate on a watch, in blocks of sixty seconds, four times an hour, and he wrote it in a notebook that was his and not the observer's. He watched her hands. Not her face — her hands. Because the face lies for a long time, and the stroke lies for longer, and the shoulder can keep turning over for an hour after the person driving it has effectively gone, but the hand tells you the truth: when the fingers come apart at the entry and stay apart, she is losing the periphery, and when the recovery arm starts to come through wide and low instead of over, the shoulder girdle is going, and when both of those things arrive within twenty minutes of each other, you have somewhere between forty and ninety minutes before you are having a different kind of night.
He had a cut-off. He had never told her what it was. He had never told the observer either, because the observer's job was not that.
The cut-off was not a number, in the end. It was: when I would rather have her alive and hate me.

He had used it once, in 2014, in the Bristol Channel, at hour nine, and she had not spoken to him for five days and had then said, in the car outside a Tesco in Newtownards, "You were right," in exactly the tone of a woman reading out an insurance policy.
And in 2016 he had not used it, because there had been nothing to use it on, because at hour twelve on the return leg of an English Channel two-way it had not been Farangis who was in trouble.

He was fifty-two. His hair had gone at the temples and he had put on the same stone she had, for none of the same reasons. He had a good career and a lot of colleagues and about three friends, and in the ten years since it happened he had been offered, by various well-meaning people, a great many opportunities to leave.
The idea that he had stayed out of nobility was, he thought, an insult to both of them.
Here is the truth, and he had arrived at it slowly, over about four years, mostly at three in the morning in a house where the other person was also awake and also pretending:

There were, at the end of everything, two people alive who had been on that boat and had loved that boy. Ailbhe Nunan had been there but she had not loved him; she had ratified him. Wilson's predecessor was dead of something ordinary in 2019. The crew were paid. So: two. Him and her.

If he left, then there would be one person on earth carrying it who was alone with it, and there would be a second person on earth carrying it who was alone with it, and the total quantity of the thing would not go down, it would double.

That was it. That was the whole of the reason. It was not love, exactly, although he loved her; it was closer to physics. Two objects at the bottom of a well, and one of them climbing out does not empty the well.
And it had a shadow, and he knew the shadow was there.

Because he did not blame her. He had never blamed her. Not for one hour, not in one argument, not once in ten years — and he had checked, he had gone looking for it in himself, deliberately, the way you press a bruise — and there was nothing there. He knew what hour nineteen of a two-way does to a swimmer's core temperature. He knew what her visual field was. He knew, because he had been the one in the water, that the interval between the shout and the boat turning was eleven seconds and that it could not have been shorter with the crew that was aboard. He knew that his son had gone under behind her, out of her sight, on a moonless night in September, and that a woman at hour nineteen with a core of thirty-four point eight is a person whose body has already been given away.
There was nothing to forgive. That was his honest, medical, twenty-one-years-of-holding-people-at-the-edge conclusion.
And he had watched, over ten years, what that conclusion did to her.

Because she needed to be forgiven, and he could not do it, because you cannot forgive a person for something they did not do — the words come out but the transaction does not complete — and every time he said there was nothing you could have done, she heard it as a man declining to give evidence.

He had understood this in about the fourth year. He had never found a way round it. He had tried, twice, to say something like it out loud, and both times it had come out as I don't blame you, which was the sentence that did the damage, and after the second time he stopped.

So they lived in a house in Bangor with a photograph of a boy in the hall, and she swam, and he greased her shoulders, and the thing they did not say to each other got older and more articulate every year.
On the Wednesday night, with the wind still wrong, he went out to the front of the guesthouse to ring the hospital about a list he was not covering, and afterwards he stood in the road for a while.
Marguerite came out to bring the bin round and said, because she was the kind of woman who said things: "She'll be all right. She's some woman for it."
"She is."
"My Stephen said the North Channel's a different animal. The jellyfish."
"Yes."
"He said the jellyfish."
"There's a lot of them," said Dariush.

Marguerite went in. He stayed out. The fog signal went on the Copelands, sixty seconds, sixty seconds, sixty seconds, and off to the north-east there was nothing to see at all, and he stood in a road in a small town and did the arithmetic he had been doing every August for ten years, which was: thirty hours, twelve degrees, forty-seven years old, eleven stone nine, and a woman who has come to the water this time not to swim across it but to make somebody say something.
He went in and did not sleep.
Sohrab at Six

The Aurora leisure centre in Bangor on a Saturday morning in 2003 had a small pool at twenty-nine degrees with a wave machine in the big pool next door that went off every twenty minutes and made everyone shout.
Sohrab was six and could not swim.

This was, in the family, a joke of such long standing that it had become a fact about him, like his ears. Her son. Her actual son. Six years old and afraid of the water, and afraid of it in the specific, unbudgeable, entirely reasonable way of a child who has once been out of his depth for two seconds and has correctly concluded that the world contains a thing that will kill you and that adults think it is fun.

She had not pushed. This was the one thing she had got right and she held onto it for the rest of her life. She had not pushed, she had not made it a project, she had not stood in the shallow end with her arms out saying come on, and she had watched other mothers do exactly that and had wanted to drown them.

What she did instead was she took him on a Saturday morning and she got in and she stood in four feet of chlorinated water at twenty-nine degrees, which is the temperature of a bath that has gone off, and she held him.

Just held him. That was the whole activity. He put his arms round her neck and his legs round her waist, which he was slightly too big for by then and would be far too big for within a year, and she walked up and down the shallow end for thirty-five minutes.

He talked the entire time. He was a talker, that child, from the moment he had words, and he talked about a boy called Ryan who had a scooter, and about whether a shark could get into a swimming pool through the filter, which he had thought about carefully and had concluded probably not but wanted a second opinion on, and about the wave machine, which he hated, and which he wanted to know the exact time of, so that they could be somewhere else.
And at some point in the fifth or sixth Saturday, in the middle of a sentence about Ryan's scooter, he took one hand off her neck and put it on her chin.

He did it to turn her face. That was all it was. He was talking and she had been looking somewhere else — at the clock, probably, because she was always looking at a clock — and a six-year-old put a small wet hand flat on her jaw and turned her head to face him and carried on the sentence.

She could still feel it. That was the honest situation, at forty-seven, and she had stopped trying to be reasonable about it. Not a metaphor, not a memory in the ordinary sense: a physical sensation, available on demand, on the left side of her jaw, of a wet hand with the fingers slightly spread, applying about as much pressure as you would use to move a cup.
She had had it during swims. She had had it in a car park in Dundonald in 2011 when her mother died. She had had it during a smear test in 2019 and had had to ask the nurse for a minute.

The pool smelled of chlorine and the wave machine went off next door and everybody shouted, and Sohrab said, "There it is, that's it, that's the one I don't like," and buried his face in her neck with an entirely theatrical wail, and she laughed, and walked him to the far end where the sound was smaller, and that was a Saturday morning in 2003, and there was nothing in it, and it is the single most valuable thing she owns.
He learned to swim at seven and a half, at his own speed, from a man called Trevor with a whistle, in a group of eight children, without her present.
She had wanted, so badly it embarrassed her, to be the one who taught him.
She had known, with total clarity, that she must not be.

And of everything she had done as a mother — every early morning, every missed thing, every hour of every year she had spent in water instead of in a house — that was the decision she was proudest of, and it had lasted nine years, and then she had put him in the English Channel at nineteen because she wanted him to see her do it.
The Ask
He asked for the first time when he was seventeen.

They were in the kitchen in Bangor and she was making up feeds for a Lough Erne swim and he was doing something to a bicycle wheel on the good table, and he said, without looking up, "Mum. Let me pace you on the Channel."
"No."
"You didn't think about it."
"I don't need to think about it."

By then he had been swimming for nine years and racing for six, and he was — this is important, and it is the part that made everything afterwards liveable and unbearable in equal measure — he was actually good. Not a prodigy. Not her. But an Ulster Schools finalist over four hundred freestyle, a boy with a proper stroke and a genuine engine, who had qualified for and completed a six-hour qualifying swim in fourteen-degree water at Lough Neagh at seventeen with two other members of the club and had got out at the end of it grinning like an idiot and eaten four sausage rolls.

He asked again at eighteen. She said no. He asked in the January he turned nineteen and she said no, and he said, "Give me the actual reason," and she said, "The actual reason is that I'm not having my son in the water at three in the morning in the middle of the English Channel," and he said, "But you'll have Kieran in the water," and she said, "Kieran is thirty-four," and he said, "Kieran does a four-fifty-eight four hundred, Mum. I do a four-nineteen."
And she had no answer to that, and he watched her not have one, and he was smart enough to leave it there and go out of the room.
She said yes in April.
Now. The reason.

The reason she gave, at the time, to Dariush, to the club, to herself, and later to two journalists, was this: he was qualified, he was fast, he was competent in cold water, the rules permit a pace swimmer for one hour in three on a two-way, the pace swimmer is never more than a few metres from a boat with four adults on it, and it is, statistically, one of the safest hours a nineteen-year-old competitive swimmer will spend in a year. All of which was true. Every word of it was true, and it is still true, and she had checked it again as recently as March.
The reason was not that.
The reason was that she wanted him to see her do it.

She was thirty-seven. She had been swimming for twenty-six years and had never once been watched by her son doing the thing she actually was. He had seen her come home. He had seen the bag and the wet costume and the kettle. He had seen a woman who was tired at breakfast and who missed his prize day in 2011 and who was, in the ordinary hours of the ordinary house, a slightly distracted person who worked part-time in a school office and had a hobby that people asked polite questions about at Christmas.
He had never seen her at hour fourteen.

And she wanted him to. She wanted her son, once, before he went to Liverpool in September and started the life in which she would become a woman he rang on Sundays, to be in the water beside her in the dark at the fourteenth hour of an English Channel two-way and to look across and see what his mother was.
That is it. That is the whole thing. There is no version of it in which she does not know exactly what she was doing.
She has said, out loud, four times in ten years, to Dariush, in the small hours, the sentence: I put him in there so he'd look at me.
And Dariush has said, four times, some version of: He was nineteen, he was a strong swimmer, and he asked you for two years.
Which is a true sentence that answers a different question.

There is an old story in it, and she knew the story, and she had known it since she was seven, because it is the story every Iranian child gets whether or not anybody in the house is religious or literary or interested: a great champion who does not know his own son, and who fights him for two days by a river, and who has, in his belt, on the second day, a knife.
She had never once told Sohrab that his name came from it.

She had told him it was his grandfather's brother's name, which was also true, and which was the reason she had given her mother-in-law in 1997, and which had the enormous advantage of not requiring her to explain to a child how the story ends.
He found out anyway, at fourteen, from a boy at school whose mother was from Shiraz, and came home and said, "Mum, do you know I'm named after somebody who gets killed?"
And she said, "Everybody's named after somebody who gets killed."
And he thought that was very funny, and repeated it for about a year.
The Last Summer
The summer of 2016 was the best year of her life and she had known it at the time, which is rare, and which is worse.

He had finished his A levels in June and had a place at Liverpool for engineering and had until the end of September, and he did not get a job, and neither of them made him, and Dariush had raised it once in April and been outvoted.
So there were fourteen weeks.

He got up at ten. He was nineteen and he got up at ten, and she was up at five, and there was a window between five and ten in which she did the whole of her training, and then she came in with her hair wet and he would be at the table eating something appalling, and she would sit down opposite him with tea and they would talk for an hour.

An hour. Every day, for fourteen weeks. She has done the arithmetic — of course she has — and it comes to somewhere near ninety hours, and it is more time than she spent talking to her son in the three years before it and infinitely more than she would have got in the thirty years after, and she has never been able to decide whether the summer was a gift or the setup for a joke.
What they talked about:
Whether the club coach was any good, which he was not, and Sohrab's four-month campaign to say so diplomatically.

A girl called Erin who worked in the Spar and whose existence was raised eleven times, obliquely, over three weeks, and then never again, and about which Farangis had asked exactly one question, at exactly the right moment, and had received exactly one answer, which was: "It's fine. It's a whole thing. Don't."

Whether their family was Iranian or Northern Irish or neither and what he was supposed to write on forms and whether he could be bothered. He had a whole routine about it that he had developed for school and that he performed for her with a level of comic control that startled her, because she had not known he had that either.
Money, briefly and unsuccessfully.
The Channel.

Because by June it was decided, and they were doing it together, and the boat was booked for the first week of September, and the training had a shape that included him in it, and this is the part that she has had to hold at arm's length for ten years because it is not survivable at close range:
He was so happy.

Not pleased. Not flattered. Happy the way a nineteen-year-old is happy about the one thing in his life that he has decided on entirely by himself and pursued for two years against opposition and got. He told the girl in the Spar. He told his uncle in Belfast twice. He put it on his phone somewhere and Farangis had never been able to find where.

He learned to feed. That was his idea; he did not want to just be a body in the water, he wanted to be crew, and he spent an afternoon in July with Dariush and a pole and a bottle in the harbour at Donaghadee learning to send a feed out on a yellow rope, and he was bad at it, and got better, and Dariush had a photograph of the two of them on the harbour wall that afternoon that lived, for ten years, in a drawer under a fuse box instruction leaflet, in an envelope, on top of a document.

In August he did a six-hour qualifier at Lough Neagh with two others from the club in fourteen-degree water, and came out and ate four sausage rolls in the car park, and rang her from the car, and said — she has this, she is sure of this, this one is intact — "Mum. That was nothing."

And she had laughed, because it was her own sentence, the one she had said on a beach at eleven with her lips blue in front of Judith Herron, and because she had never told him about that, and because there is a thing that comes down the generations without anybody putting it there.
That was nothing.
She said: "It's not nothing. Don't say that."
And he said: "You say it."
And she said: "That's how I know."

Five weeks later he went into the English Channel at hour eighteen of a two-way with a green cap on, or possibly an orange one, and swam beside his mother for an hour and twenty-two minutes, in the dark, breathing every two on the left so that they were face to face on every second stroke, which was not standard, which was a thing he had started doing, and which she had not told him to stop.
Taper
Three days without swimming.

The physiology of a taper is uncontroversial and mildly boring: you stop doing the volume, glycogen stores supercompensate, the small structural damage in the muscle repairs, and you arrive at the start line with a body that is, measurably, better than the body that finished the last hard session. Everyone agrees. It works. It is the least interesting true thing in sport.
The psychology of a taper is that you lose your mind.

Consider what has been removed. For eleven months she has swum between forty and seventy kilometres a week. That is between fourteen and twenty-two hours in the water.
