It is not a hobby and it is not exercise; it is the load-bearing structure of the day, and everything else in the twenty-four hours has been arranged around it and downstream of it. The swimming produced the appetite, the sleep, the mood, the ability to sit in a room with other people and appear normal. Take it out and what is left is a forty-seven-year-old woman in a rented room in Donaghadee with an enormous unspent metabolism and a mind that has not been made to sit still since 1990.

By the second day her hands would not stay still on the table. By the third she had walked the length of the front eleven times before ten in the morning, slowly, deliberately slowly, because walking fast is exercise and exercise is not permitted, which meant that the only physical activity available to her was a slow walk, which is to a marathon swimmer roughly what a lozenge is to a smoker.
She could not read. She read the same four pages of a paperback of Marguerite's about a woman inheriting a house in France.
She could not watch anything.
She was unbearable, and she knew she was unbearable, and knowing it did not help, and Dariush had learned in 2009 that the correct response was to be in the same building but not the same room.
And underneath the restlessness there was the thing the taper actually is, which is the removal of the anaesthetic.

Because that is what the volume is for. Nobody who swims seventy kilometres a week is doing it for the training effect; the training effect maxes out well below that. They are doing it because at twenty hours a week you are, functionally, unconscious for a fifth of your waking life, and it is a very particular quality of unconsciousness, and you cannot get it any other way, and when you stop, everything you have been putting under it comes up in about thirty-six hours, like a body in a lake.
On the Thursday she sat on the end of the bed at four in the afternoon for fifty minutes without moving.
Now: the switch.

There is a mental technique at the centre of this sport and it is genuinely a technique, teachable, and Farangis could teach it, and had, to about nine people over the years, and had watched four of them get it and five of them not.
The rule is: you never swim the channel.

The channel is thirty-four and a half kilometres and it is unswimmable, in the sense that no human mind can hold it. Hold the whole distance in your head at hour four and you will get out. Everybody who has ever got out and been unable to say why afterwards got out because for one moment they saw the whole thing at once.
So you do not swim the channel. You swim to the feed.

Thirty minutes. That is the unit. That is the largest object permitted inside the mind. At any moment in a thirty-hour swim there are, at most, thirty minutes of future, and generally rather fewer, and when the bottle comes back in on the line the clock resets and there are thirty minutes again, and the whole crossing is not a crossing at all, it is a chain of sixty small identical rooms, and you are only ever in one of them.

Beneath the feed there is the stroke count, which is finer. Four hundred. That is her number and has been since 2004. She counts to four hundred and then she starts again, and four hundred strokes at sixty a minute is six minutes and forty seconds, and there are four and a half of them in a feed cycle, and she does not count the cycles, because counting the cycles is counting the channel.

Beneath the stroke count there is the stroke, which is the smallest room of all and the only one that is actually real. Hand enters at eleven o'clock, fingertips first, no slap. Extend forward under the surface, not down. Catch: the forearm comes vertical while the elbow stays high, which is the single hardest thing to hold when you are tired and the first thing to go. Press back. Exit at the hip. Recover over. Breathe every two on the left in a calm sea, every three when she wants to see both sides, every two on the right when the wind comes round.
That is the entire content of thirty hours.
People ask what you think about. The answer, from every swimmer who is telling the truth, is: nothing, and then, later, whatever is in you, whether or not you have consented to it.

Because the technique has a limit, and the limit is roughly hour fourteen. Up to fourteen the discipline holds and the mind stays in the small room. After fourteen, in the dark, hypoglycaemic, with the core down a degree and a half, the doors between the rooms come off their hinges. And what arrives is not chosen. Swimmers report, in a literature that is now large and remarkably consistent: conversations with the boat crew that the boat crew did not have; the certainty of being able to see the seabed in two thousand metres of water; music; the smell of specific rooms; the dead.
And the third man. The presence. Somebody swimming alongside, on the far side from the boat, in the black, matching the stroke.

She had had it twice. Once in the Kaiwi Channel in 2013, where it had been benign and vaguely male and had stayed for about ninety minutes and had gone. Once off Robben Island in 2017 for about twenty minutes.
She had never told anyone what she had done, in 2017, when it came.
She had turned her head to the left, in the dark, in the sea, at hour nine, and she had said his name out loud into the water.

And it had not answered, because they do not answer, because it is a construction of a hypoxic, hypothermic, sensorily starved brain doing the only thing brains do, which is to insist that there is somebody there.
She had been trying to get back to it for nine years.

This is the thing she had never admitted to anybody in any form, and which she was going to have to admit in about thirty hours to a woman with a clipboard: she did not train for the North Channel because it was the last of a set. She trained for the North Channel because it is thirty-plus hours, and thirty-plus hours in twelve degrees is the longest available dose, and she had come to believe — not intellectually, she was not stupid, but somewhere lower down and much more powerful than the intellect — that if she got deep enough into it, if she went far enough out along that particular axis, she would get an hour with her son.
It is not a rational belief.
Neither is anything else that gets a person into the North Channel.
At twenty past nine on the Thursday evening the phone rang and it was Wilson and he said: "Nought two hundred. Harbour at half one."

And she stood up, and everything that had been coming up out of the lake for three days went back down, instantly, cleanly, like a light going off in a room she was leaving anyway, and she felt — she could feel it happening — the person she needed to be for the next day and a half come up through her body and take the controls.
"Right," she said.
Nought Two Hundred

Donaghadee harbour at one in the morning in the first week of August. Air fourteen degrees. Water twelve point one. No moon to speak of, and a high thin cloud, and the town entirely asleep behind them except for the lights on the lifeboat station and one window somewhere up on the hill.

The boat was a converted fishing boat called Kestrel Star with a wheelhouse and a lit deck and a smell of diesel and old rope, and it was already loaded: the flask crate, the feed bottles in two milk crates lashed under the gunwale, the glow sticks, the spare goggles, four caps, the medical bag Dariush never opened and always brought, the two lights on the port side that would be pointed at her for twenty-nine hours, and a length of yellow rope with a bottle carrier on the end of it that had made forty-one crossings of various kinds and had a name, which was Gerald, for a reason that had been lost in about 2011.
Wilson had a crew of two: a nephew called Ryan, who was nineteen and silent, and a man of about fifty called Dessie who had done this eighty times.

Ailbhe Nunan came down the steps at twenty past one with the canvas bag and set up on the port side under the wheelhouse where she could see the whole of the swimmer's water. She wrote the date at the top of the sheet. She wrote the air temperature. She wrote the sea state. She checked her watch against the boat's clock and against her phone and made a note of the discrepancy, which was four seconds, because that is the job.
Farangis stood at the top of the harbour steps in a costume and a towel and let her husband do her shoulders for the last time.

He did it in silence. Neck, traps, delts, the strap line, the armpits, the inside of the upper arms where they would rub against the ribs forty thousand times. He put a second coat over the zinc on the back of her neck where the sun would come at hour six if there was any. He greased her jaw where the goggle strap ran.
She said, "Don't do my face."
"I'm not doing your face."
"You're doing my face."
"I'm doing the strap."
"Right."

He finished. He capped the tub. There was about a minute left and neither of them had anything prepared, because in twenty-five years they had never once had anything prepared, because the correct thing to say before a Channel swim does not exist and everyone who tries to invent it produces something that sits in the swimmer's head for thirty hours like a stone in a shoe.
So he said: "Eighty a hour."
"Eighty a hour."
"Take the feeds even when you don't want them. Especially at fourteen and especially at twenty."
"Yes."
"If you turn away from the bottle twice in a row I'm going to shout at you, and you're going to think I'm being a bully, and I'm going to keep doing it."
"I know."
"Farangis."
"What."

He had his hands on her shoulders. They had been there for perhaps twenty seconds longer than the greasing required, and both of them knew what the next four minutes contained and that this was the last of it.
"Nothing," he said. "Go on."
He took his hands off.

She went down the steps. On the third from the bottom, where the weed was, she stopped, and turned, and he was at the top with the tub in one hand and his palms out from his body, shining, and behind him the whole small dark town.
"See you in a bit," she said.
He did not answer, because if he answered it would come out wrong.

She put the goggles on and pulled the cap down and stood in the wash for a second with the water at her ankles, and then she walked in until it was at her thighs and then she put her hands together and went.
At 02:00:04 by the observer's watch she cleared the water line and began swimming, and Ailbhe Nunan wrote 02:00 START — swimmer clear, no assistance on a sheet of paper in a boat.
The rule was live.
For the next thirty-one hours and forty minutes, no human being would be permitted to touch Farangis Roshanfar.
PART TWO — DAYLIGHT
Hour One
The first thing is that it is not cold.

It is never cold at the start. This surprises people and it should not: the body has fifteen or twenty minutes of stored heat in the shell before the shell gives it up, and the entry produces a flood of catecholamines that would mask a broken arm, and the first hour of any swim is the best hour of any swim and always will be. She had known swimmers who spent the whole of their careers chasing hour one and got out at hour six every time, disappointed, as though something had been withheld from them.
Air fourteen. Water twelve point one. Stroke rate sixty-two.

The harbour lights went behind and the boat came up on her left at about a hundred metres and settled there, and Wilson found the line he wanted and held it, and that was the arrangement for the next day and a half: the swimmer to starboard of the boat, three to five metres off, the boat's two lamps angled down into her water, everyone on deck able to see her and nobody able to reach her.

The water at night is not black. That is the first correction. Under a lit boat it is a dense translucent brown-green, and it has depth, in the sense that the light penetrates two or three metres and then stops, so what you are looking at is a lit room with no floor. Her right arm came into the frame at eleven o'clock, fingertips first, and pushed a small wake of bubbles down its length, and the bubbles hung in the lit water and came back past her hip and were gone, and then her left arm, and then her right.
Forty thousand times.
The mechanics, then, because the mechanics are the book, and everything that happens later happens on top of them.

Her stroke was long and it was old-fashioned. She had been taught by a woman who had been taught in the 1960s, and she had never fully converted to the high-turnover, shorter-lever stroke that pool swimming went to in the nineties, and in a channel this was an advantage: fewer strokes per kilometre means fewer shoulder rotations, and the shoulder is the thing that ends most attempts. She turned over at sixty-two in flat water and would drop to fifty-six by hour twelve and would be at forty-nine by hour twenty-four, and the drop was expected and mapped and Dariush would write each number in his notebook and compare it to a curve he had drawn in 2015.

Breathing every two, left side. This is what marathon swimmers do and what pool coaches spend years trying to stop children doing. Bilateral breathing — every three, alternating — is better for symmetry and better for sighting and worse for oxygen, and after about six hours nobody cares about symmetry. So: left, left, left, forty thousand times, which means the right shoulder does more work in the rotation and the left side of the neck does all of the turning, and by hour twenty the neck is a hinge that has been asked to do something a hinge should not be asked to do.

Hence the grease. Hence the zinc on the jaw. The chafe points on a marathon swimmer are absolutely predictable and are the same on every swimmer of every size: the sides of the neck where the chin turns, the armpits, the inside of the upper arms, the bikini line, and — for women — under the arm where the costume edge sits. Untreated, in salt water, over thirty hours, these do not blister; they abrade. The salt goes into the abrasion and the abrasion goes on being rubbed sixty times a minute for another eighteen hours, and by the finish there are people who cannot put a shirt on for four days.

Sighting: almost none. This is the strange freedom of a piloted swim and the reason a channel swim is nothing like a race. She did not need to know where she was going. Wilson knew where she was going. Her entire navigational responsibility for thirty hours was to stay within about five metres of a boat that was on her left, which she could do on feel and sound alone, and which she monitored perhaps four times an hour with a lifted head.
She was, in the most literal sense, being driven.

There was a freedom in that so total that it verged on the obscene, and it was one of the reasons she was there, and she had never found a way to describe it that did not make her sound like a woman describing a sedative.
At 02:32 the first feed went out on the pole.

Dessie held it. Dariush would take over at feed four, because Dessie was better at the first ones and Dariush was better at the ones after hour ten, and this had been worked out in the Bristol Channel in 2014 and never revisited.
She rolled onto her back for two seconds, took the bottle, drank two hundred and fifty millilitres of warm maltodextrin in eleven seconds, said "Good," and let go.
"Twenty-two seconds," said Dariush, to Ailbhe.
Ailbhe wrote it down.
"Feed one, twenty-two seconds," she said. "Twelve one. Stroke rate sixty-two. Swimmer's condition good."

And underneath that, in the second column, in the space reserved for the observer's own remarks, she wrote nothing at all, and looked out at the woman in the water for a while, and then looked at the shape of the man standing at the rail with a pole in his hand and his coat collar up.
Feed Four

By 04:00 they had cleared the Copelands and were out into the channel proper, and the swell came round — nothing, half a metre, a long slow lift and drop with about eight seconds in it — and the boat began to work, and Ryan the nephew was sick over the stern twice and said nothing about it and went on coiling rope.

This is a fact that swimmers find funny and never stop finding funny: the crew get seasick and the swimmer does not. There is no such thing as a seasick marathon swimmer. The vestibular apparatus does not complain when the body is horizontal and in the medium; the nausea of a channel swim comes from sugar and salt and cold, never from motion. So the standard arrangement is a woman in the water at hour twelve feeling reasonably well, and four adults on a boat six feet away, in coats, on a warm deck, with food and tea and a lavatory, feeling considerably worse than she does.
Farangis had been the least ill person present at every significant event of her adult life.
Feed four. Dariush took the pole.

There is a whole language on the pole. The feeder cannot touch and mostly cannot hear — a swimmer's ears are full of water and the boat's engine is running at fifteen hundred revs three metres away — so the exchange is compressed to about six words and a set of gestures that a crew develops over years.
"Time?" she said. It is the standard first question and every swimmer asks it and every good feeder lies about it in a specific direction.
"Two hours," said Dariush.

It was two hours and four minutes. He always rounded down early in a swim, because early in a swim the elapsed time is a burden, and rounded up late in a swim, because late in a swim the elapsed time is currency.
"Where's the tide."
"Turns at ten past six. You're carrying it."
"Right."
"Take the whole bottle."
She took the whole bottle.
He watched her hands as she gave it back. Fingers together on the release. Good.

She put her face down and went, and he pulled Gerald in on the yellow rope and stowed the bottle in the crate for the empties and wrote 04:00 / 250 / 19s / all in his notebook, and then, out of a habit twenty-five years old and entirely useless, he checked his watch against the stars, which were not visible, and put his hands back in his pockets.
Ailbhe said, from under the wheelhouse: "You round down."
"I do."
"I've seen a feeder round down by an hour and a half at hour twenty."
"That's not rounding, that's fraud."
"It's a spectrum," said Ailbhe.

It was the first time in ten years and two months that the two of them had said anything to each other that was not administrative, and both of them noticed it, and neither of them followed it up, and the boat went on north-east at two and a half kilometres an hour into the dark.
Hour Three
At 05:10, in the last of the true dark, she saw something at her left shoulder in the glare of the boat's lamp.

It was nothing. It resolved instantly into what it was, which was the edge of the lit water where the lamp's cone ended and the brown-green went to black, a moving boundary that travelled with her at exactly her own speed because it was made by a light that was on a boat that was going her speed. She had been swimming beside that boundary for eleven years. It was as familiar as a skirting board.
She saw it and something in her chest went off like a starter's pistol.

That was all. A half-second. The rate went up and the stroke shortened and she took three strokes that were not her stroke, and then she had it back, and she put her face down and counted to four hundred.
It is worth saying what happened there, physiologically, because it is going to happen again and it is going to matter.

The startle was not a mistake. She had not mistaken a shadow for a person. She had seen a shadow, correctly identified it as a shadow, and had a full autonomic response anyway, which is the ordinary functioning of a nervous system in which a specific stimulus — the appearance of a shape at the left shoulder, in water, at night — has been paired with the worst outcome available to a human animal.
Ten years. Not one swim in ten years without it.

She had done the work. That is the thing that never gets into the profiles. She had done eleven months of a trauma-focused therapy in 2018 with a woman in Belfast who was excellent, and she had done the exposure work, and she had done it honestly and completely, and it had helped, substantially and permanently, with almost everything.
It had not touched the shoulder.

The therapist had told her at the end, with the frankness Farangis had paid for, that there were two possible reasons. The first was that the stimulus was not extinguishable because she went on presenting herself with it at forty times a year with the full physiological arousal profile intact — that she was, in effect, re-consolidating the association every time she got in the sea, and that the treatment for that was to stop swimming, and that she was not going to stop swimming, and that they both knew it.
The second was that extinction requires the memory to be available for updating, and that hers was not, because there was a hole in it.
Eleven seconds.

The therapist had wanted to work on the eleven seconds. Farangis had gone twice more and then stopped going, and had told Dariush that they had finished the course, which was true in the way that things she said to Dariush were true.

At 05:40 the sky over the Scottish side went from black to a very dark blue with no event in between, and by 06:00 there was a grey light on the water, and the lamps were switched off, and the world had a horizon in it again, and the boat turned out to be a boat rather than a shape with lights on it, and Ryan the nephew turned out to have red hair.
"Sun's up," said Dariush at the feed.
"I noticed."
"Twelve point one still."
"It doesn't feel it."
"That's because you've been in three and a half hours."
"That's cheerful."
"You asked."
"I didn't ask," said Farangis.

She looked at him for a moment, treading, with her goggles up on her forehead and her face the particular grey-white that grease and cold produce and that photographs so badly that swimmers' families are always shocked by the pictures.
"Dariush."
"What?"

The boat rose and fell. The gap between them was three metres of water and it was, for the next twenty-six hours, uncrossable, and both of them were entirely aware of this at all times and had been for a day and a half.
"Nothing," she said.
Hour Four
At 06:10 the tide turned, and the whole geometry of the day changed, and this is the part that outsiders never grasp and that decides everything.

Until 06:10 the flood had been running north and she had been ferried up-channel while crossing it, so her track over the ground was a long diagonal to the north-east, and the distance made good towards Scotland was less than the distance swum by a factor of about a third. Now the ebb came in and everything reversed: the water began to run south, at first slowly, then at one knot, then at a bit under two through the middle, and the track over the ground bent the other way.

The plot, if you saw it afterwards, was an elongated S lying on its side. Everybody's is. The art of piloting a channel is to make the two arms of the S the same length so they cancel, and to have the swimmer arrive at the far coast at the moment of slack, because if she arrives half an hour late the tide takes her past the headland and she has to swim the last two kilometres across a current that is going faster than she is, and that is where swims die: not in the middle, at the end, four hundred metres off Scotland, going sideways.
Which meant that from 06:10 Wilson was steering a course that made no visual sense whatsoever.

Farangis lifted her head at 06:20 and saw the Scottish coast — actually saw it for the first time, a low grey-blue line to the east, closer than it had any right to be — and saw that the boat was pointing about thirty degrees to the left of it.
At 06:30, feed nine, she said: "We're going north."
"We're crabbing," said Dariush.
"I can see the coast."
"You can see a coast. It's not your coast. Your coast is Portpatrick and it's further right and Wilson wants you high because the ebb's going to walk you down about four kilometres before slack."
"It feels wrong."
"It is wrong. It's wrong in the correct direction. Take the whole bottle."
She took the whole bottle.
This is the least discussed and most absolute of the sport's requirements, and it is not physical.
You have to hand over your judgment.

At hour four you are lucid, you are strong, you can see the land, and a man you have known for three summers is steering you away from it, and you are going to swim in the direction he indicates for another twenty-five hours on the basis of nothing but a chart, an almanac, and his forty years. There is no version of this in which you get to check. You cannot see the current. The current is invisible by definition; a body in a moving fluid has no way of detecting the motion of the fluid. You are inside the problem and you are made of the same water as the problem.
So you trust the boat.

And there is a specific perversity in it, which is that the sport is sold, in every article ever written about it, as the ultimate individual endeavour, the human alone against the sea, self-reliance, the unassisted crossing — and the truth is that from the moment you go in you are an instrument being operated by a man in a wheelhouse, and the only thing you actually control is whether your hand goes in at eleven o'clock.

Farangis had thought about this a great deal. She had concluded, some time around 2015, that the sport was not about self-reliance at all. It was about a very rare and very extreme form of dependence, dressed up in the language of its opposite, and that the people who were drawn to it were not people who wanted to be alone but people who could not tolerate being helped in the ordinary way, at ordinary distances, by ordinary means — and who had therefore found the one arrangement on earth in which the help arrives at exactly three metres, and never any closer, and never touches you, and cannot.
She had not said this to anybody either.
She put her head down and swam thirty degrees left of Scotland for two hours.

At 08:30, feed thirteen, the sun got over the cloud and came in low and hard from the south-east and lit the whole channel a hard silver, and everything went white in the goggles on the breathing side, and for a while she swam blind on the left and turned her head to the right, breathing every three to alternate, and Dariush wrote 08:30 switched to bilateral, glare in his notebook, and Ailbhe wrote 08:30 stroke rate 60. Swimmer alert. Water 12.0. Sea state 2. Condition: good.
And in the second column, the one for the observer's own remarks, Ailbhe Nunan wrote, for the first time that day:
Ten years since I last watched this swimmer.
And then she looked at it for a while, and then she scored it out, twice, until it could not be read.
The Rule

At seven in the morning, with the sun up and the swimmer settled into the fifth hour and nothing to do for twenty-three minutes, Ryan the nephew asked the question that every person who has ever crewed a marathon swim asks in their first ten hours.
He asked it of the deck generally, in the way nineteen-year-olds do, so that it could be withdrawn.
"What if she was drowning, but."
Nobody answered for a moment.
Dessie was coiling something. Wilson was in the wheelhouse. Dariush was writing a number in a notebook.
"Then we'd get her out," said Dessie.
"And it's over."
"It's over."
"So she'd rather drown."
"No," said Ailbhe Nunan, without looking up. "She'd rather we got her out. She'd just rather we didn't have to."
The boy thought about that and did not get it, which is correct, because it takes about four years.
Here is the argument, and it is worth setting down properly, because the whole book is inside it.

The rule is not a rule about safety. Everybody assumes it is a rule about safety and it is the opposite of a rule about safety. It is a rule that makes an already dangerous activity considerably more dangerous, deliberately, and it has survived a hundred and fifty years of people pointing that out.

The rule descends from Webb, who in 1875 swam from Dover to Calais in twenty-one hours and forty-five minutes in a silk costume with nothing on him but porpoise oil, and who was accompanied by boats, and who was not held up by any of them. Everything since is an elaboration of that: no artificial aid to buoyancy, warmth, or propulsion; no touching the escort; no touching the swimmer; one costume, one cap, one pair of goggles, grease, and a light for night. The sport calls it the unassisted crossing, and it defends the definition with an intensity that people outside find comic until they look closely.
Because here is the thing they discover when they look closely: the sport is not defending a tradition. It is defending the only thing it has.

There is no track. There is no timing gate. There is no way to compare a crossing done in flat water on a neap with a crossing done in a metre of chop on the edge of springs, and there is no way to compare either of them with a crossing done by a twenty-five-year-old and a crossing done by a woman of forty-seven. Every marathon swim is a different event conducted in a different medium under different conditions and it can never be repeated, not even by the same swimmer, not even the following week.
So the sport cannot measure. It can only certify. And the only thing it can certify is a negative: that nothing was added.

Everything else — the times, the routes, the lists, the rankings, the whole apparatus — is decoration on top of a single verifiable claim, which is: this person crossed this water and nobody helped her.

Take away the prohibition on contact and there is nothing left. Not a diminished sport. Nothing. A wetsuit crossing is a fine athletic achievement and it is a different activity with a different name, and everybody involved is entirely relaxed about that, and the two communities get on perfectly well, and neither pretends to be the other.
Now the second half of the argument, which is where it stops being administrative.
Because the rule does not merely forbid the swimmer from being helped. It forbids the crew from helping. And those are not the same prohibition, and the second one is the one that does the work.

A rule against assistance could have been written to bind the swimmer alone: she may not accept help. That would have been sufficient for verification. It is not what was written. What was written binds everyone on the boat, and it binds them absolutely, in circumstances that are foreseeable and that recur on every single crossing: the swimmer visibly suffering, visibly cold, visibly failing, three metres away, for hours.
The sport looked at that and did not carve out an exception, and has been asked to about once a decade for a hundred and fifty years, and has said no every time.

The stated reason is that any exception is unverifiable. If a hand may be laid on a swimmer in an emergency, then every crossing contains an unanswerable question about whether the hand that was laid was necessary, and the certificate is worthless. That reason is correct and it is not the real reason.
The real reason, which nobody in the sport will say out loud in a room with a journalist in it, is that the prohibition is the content.

They are not swimming across water. Anybody can be transported across water. What is being demonstrated, and what is being certified in eleven pages by a woman with a clipboard, is a specific and rather terrible proposition: that a human being can be surrounded by people who love her, in full view, within arm's reach, for a day and a half, and be entirely alone.
Not abandoned. Attended. Attended with total competence and total attention by people who would die for her and who are forbidden to reach.
That is the artefact. That is what the sport makes. Everything else is logistics.

Dariush Roshanfar had worked this out somewhere around 2011 and had never told his wife, because he had also worked out the corollary, and the corollary was that he had married a woman who had gone looking, at eleven years old, on a beach in County Down, for exactly that arrangement, and had found it, and had spent thirty-six years perfecting her access to it.
"It's not that she'd rather drown," he said to the boy, eventually. "It's that she's spent her whole life looking for a room where nobody can get to her, and this is the only one that's legal."
Ryan looked at him.
"That's fucking grim," he said.
"Yes," said Dariush. "Take the pole for a minute, I need to sit down."
Sohrab at Fourteen
The year he got fast was 2011.

Nothing had indicated it. He had been a decent age-grouper, top eight at Ulster level, the kind of swimmer a club is glad to have and does not build a season around, and then between March and October of his fourteenth year he grew five inches and his four hundred freestyle went from five minutes and eleven to four minutes and thirty-six.

Coaches call it the window and they are careful about it because it closes. A boy at fourteen with a new lever length and a new heart is briefly a different animal, and if the technique is already sound the times fall off a cliff, and then puberty finishes and the ones who were only ever early stop improving and the ones who were actually good keep going. Nobody knows which is which until about seventeen.
He came out of the water at the Ulster Age Groups in October 2011 having done a four thirty-six and looked at the board and then looked for her in the gallery.

She was in the gallery. She had come. This mattered, because she had missed the March meet for a qualifier in Cork and had missed the June meet for reasons she could no longer reconstruct, and she had come to this one and had sat on a plastic bench in thirty-degree air among two hundred parents for four and a half hours and had watched her son swim eight lengths.

He found her. He held up both hands with the fingers spread — some private thing they had, which meant nothing, which had started as a joke in a car — and she held up both hands with the fingers spread, and he laughed and went to get his tracksuit.
And what she felt, sitting on a plastic bench in a leisure centre in Bangor in October 2011, watching her fourteen-year-old son's time go up on a board, was this:
She felt proud, which took about a second and a half.
And then, underneath it and entirely without permission, she felt a fast, hot, complete stab of envy so pure that it made her sit up straight.

Because four thirty-six is a good four hundred, and four thirty-six at fourteen is a very good four hundred, and Farangis Roshanfar's lifetime best over four hundred metres freestyle, set in a twenty-five metre pool in Dublin in the spring of 2001 at the age of twenty-two, at the absolute peak of a career she had already privately understood was not going to go anywhere, was four minutes and forty-one seconds.
Her son had beaten her by five seconds. At fourteen. In a heat. Without particularly trying.
She sat on the bench with the envy going through her like a swallow of spirits and she thought, in words, in her own voice, the sentence: I did that for eleven years and you did it in eight months.
And then, arriving right behind it, close enough to be the same thought, she thought: and I could put you in the sea and you'd be nothing.

That is the sentence. That is the actual sentence, in her own voice, in her own head, on a plastic bench, about a fourteen-year-old boy who was at that moment pulling a tracksuit over wet shoulders and looking for her again.
She has never told anybody that sentence.

She has told Dariush that she was jealous. She has said it lightly, as a joke, more than once, and it goes down well because it is charming when a mother says she is jealous of her son, it is one of the permitted forms of love. What she has not said, and what is true, is that within a second and a half of her son's best swim she had located the arena in which she could still beat him and had privately gone there for comfort.
And here is why it matters, and why she has spent ten years going round it:
That was 2011. He was fourteen. He first asked to swim the Channel with her at seventeen. She said no for two years. She said yes at nineteen.
And she cannot now, and will never be able to, establish to her own satisfaction how much of the yes came out of the thing she thought on that bench.

She has been over it ten thousand times. She has constructed a defence and she can deliver it: the sentence was involuntary, it was one second of a normal human nervous system doing an ugly thing, everybody has them, the fact that she remembers it at all is evidence that she found it appalling, and there is no mechanism by which a stray thought in 2011 steers a decision in 2016.

And then the prosecution stands up, and the prosecution is very quiet, and it says: you wanted him in the water so he would look at you. You have admitted that. You have said it out loud four times. So the only question is whether you also wanted him in a place where you were the better animal, and you cannot answer that question, because there is nobody alive who can look inside a mother and issue a finding, and because the only witness who could have told you what he saw when he looked across at you at hour nineteen is at the bottom of the English Channel.

At 10:30 in the North Channel, at feed seventeen, with the sun high and the water at twelve point two, Farangis Roshanfar took a bottle off a yellow line and drank two hundred and fifty millilitres and said "Good" and let go, and Ailbhe Nunan wrote feed 17, 18 seconds, all taken, condition good on a sheet of paper.
Hour Six
At 08:00 the cold started winning small arguments.

This is not a moment. That is the first thing to understand about hypothermia in a trained swimmer: there is no moment. There is a slope, and the slope is very shallow, and the person on it is the last to know because the instrument used to detect it is the thing being degraded.
The measurable stuff first.

Core temperature in a swimmer of her insulation in twelve degrees does not crash; it settles. Metabolic heat production at her workload is high — she was, in effect, doing a hard aerobic session continuously for a day and a half — and for the first several hours production and loss are close enough that the core holds at thirty-six and a half or so. Then the arithmetic tips. Glycogen depletion reduces the heat you can make; cold diuresis reduces plasma volume; the shell, which has been vasoconstricted for hours, starts to leak because vasoconstriction is not free and the smooth muscle fatigues. So from hour six the curve begins to bend, and it bends slowly, and the loss is on the order of a tenth of a degree an hour, and a tenth of a degree an hour for twenty-four hours is the entire difference between a woman swimming and a woman being lifted onto a deck.
The hands go first and go in a fixed order and she could have narrated it.
Hour two: fingers cold, fine.
Hour four: fingers cold, sensation dull at the tips, grip on the bottle still normal.

Hour six: this. The claw beginning. Not a cramp — an inability. The fingers wanted to sit slightly apart at the entry, and holding them together took an act of attention, and an act of attention is a thing you have a finite supply of and are going to want later.
Hour ten: the release of the feed bottle becomes a thing you have to plan.
Hour sixteen: the hand is a paddle. It does not close. She would take the bottle by trapping it between both palms.
Hour twenty-two: she would not be able to feel the bottle at all and would judge by sight whether she had it.

The stroke degrades accordingly and it degrades in a signature. The catch is the first casualty: holding a high elbow with a vertical forearm requires the small stabilisers of the shoulder girdle and fine proprioceptive feedback from the hand, and when the hand goes quiet and the shoulder is tired the arm drops through the water instead of pressing back against it, which is called dropping the elbow and which every swimmer has been shouted at about since they were eight. The efficiency loss is enormous — a swimmer with a dropped elbow at hour twenty is doing eighty per cent of the work for sixty per cent of the propulsion — and there is nothing to be done about it, because the fix requires exactly the resources that are gone.

She knew all of this. She had known it since she was twenty-five. Knowing it does not confer any advantage whatsoever, and this is one of the sport's small cruelties: there is no expertise that helps. The eleventh crossing hurts the same as the first. The only thing experience buys you is the ability to predict, with great precision, exactly how bad it is about to get, which is not obviously a benefit.
At 08:30 she noticed that she had counted to four hundred twice without registering either.
At 09:15 she noticed that the water had a smell, which was impossible, because she was in it, and because you cannot smell anything through a nose that is being flooded sixty times a minute.

It smelled of a kitchen. Specifically, and unmistakably, and with total sensory conviction, of the kitchen of the house in Bangor at about four in the afternoon in the winter, with the immersion heater on and something with cumin in it going on the hob.
She logged it. She had a category for it, which was hour nine stuff, arriving early, and she noted the arriving early with mild professional interest and put her face back down.

At 10:00 she began, without any decision being made, to breathe every two on the left again, and to hold, at the top of each breath, for a fraction longer than the stroke required, so that the head stayed turned for perhaps a tenth of a second more than it needed to.
She was checking her left side.

She did not notice that she was doing it. Dariush, watching her hands from a boat three metres away with a stopwatch and a notebook and twenty-five years, noticed it at 10:20 and wrote it down and did not say anything to anybody.
Wilson
Every channel has three or four people who decide who crosses it, and they are not the swimmers.

Wilson had been on the water since he was fourteen, first with his father, who fished, and then on his own account when the fishing stopped being a thing a man could feed a family on. He had come to piloting in 1988 by the ordinary route, which is that somebody asked him to take a boat out with a lunatic swimming beside it and he said yes because it was August and there was nothing else on.
He had put fifty-one people onto the Scottish shore. It is the highest number of any working pilot in the channel and he did not know the figure and would have been mildly irritated to be told it.
His success rate — the number he did know, because the association published it, and because swimmers rang him about it — was a shade over thirty-six per cent.
Which sounds terrible until you learn that the channel average is about twenty-two.
Here is what a pilot actually does, and almost none of it is steering.

He decides whether you go. That is ninety per cent of it. He has the tide tables and the almanac and four decades of local knowledge about what the sea does in the gap between the Copelands and Portpatrick in an August high, and he sits in a kitchen in Donaghadee and looks at a swimmer who has spent thirty thousand pounds and eleven months of her life and taken two weeks off work, and who is standing in front of him at forty-seven years of age with the whole thing in her hands, and he tells her no.
That is the job. Everything else is a boat.

He had told Farangis no in 2023, on a Thursday, with a forecast that most pilots would have gone on. She had driven home to Bangor that afternoon and had not spoken for two days and had rung him on the Sunday to apologise for something she had said in the kitchen, and he had said he did not remember it, which was a lie, and a kind one, and both of them knew it.

Three weeks later a swimmer had gone out of Donaghadee on a similar forecast with a different pilot and had been pulled at eleven hours in a sea that came up two hours earlier than the model said it would, and had been extremely lucky.

Wilson had not mentioned it. He never mentioned them. There is a version of the pilot who collects these stories and tells them in the kitchen to make a point, and that version is common, and Wilson was not it.
What he was instead was almost entirely silent, which swimmers found unnerving in the first year and came to understand in the third, because the silence is not temperament. It is method.

A pilot who talks is a pilot who is managing the swimmer's morale, and a pilot who is managing the swimmer's morale is a pilot who has entered into a relationship in which he will one day have to lie, and the day he lies is the day the whole arrangement fails, because the swimmer's entire safety rests on the proposition that the man in the wheelhouse is reporting the sea accurately.

So he did not encourage. He did not tell people they were doing well. He did not say nearly there, which is the single most destructive sentence available on a boat and which crews say constantly, at hour eight, and which has ended more swims than weather.
He said, when asked, the distance, the time, and the state of the tide, and he said it the same way at hour four and hour twenty-eight.
He had two rules of his own, on top of the association's.

The first was that he would not tell a swimmer she was going to make it. Ever. Under any circumstances. Not at four hundred metres. A swimmer who has been told she is going to make it stops swimming and starts arriving, and the North Channel has taken people off the shore at three hundred metres with an ebb that came round the headland, and he had watched it happen to a Frenchwoman in 2009 who had been told, by a very well-meaning man on her own crew, that she had done it.

The second was that he decided when it was over, and not the swimmer, and not the swimmer's husband, and not a doctor, and he told every crew this once, in the kitchen, in the same sentence, and did not repeat it.
"It's my boat and it's my call, and if I make it you'll not argue with me on the water. You can argue with me in the harbour."
At about eleven in the morning, at hour nine, with the swimmer running well and the tide behaving, Ailbhe Nunan came and stood in the wheelhouse door.
"You've done her three times now," she said.
"Four. There was one in twenty-two we never got in the water."
"What do you make of her."
Wilson looked at the water for a while.

There are perhaps forty people in the world qualified to answer that question and he was one of them, and the answer he gave was not the answer Ailbhe expected, and she thought about it for the next nineteen hours.
"She's the best cold-water swimmer that's ever come out of this town," he said, "and she's not here for the swim, and I've known that since the day she rang me, and I took the booking anyway."
"Why?"
"Because she'd have got somebody else," said Wilson. "And somebody else wouldn't have known."
The Drawer
The drawer is in the back bedroom, in a desk that came from her mother's house in 2011, under the fuse box instructions and the manual for a dishwasher they got rid of in 2018.

In the drawer there is an envelope with the association's crest on it. In the envelope there is an eleven-page log, and a covering letter of four lines, and a photograph of a man and a boy on the harbour wall at Donaghadee in July 2016 with a pole and a yellow rope, which Dariush put in there in October 2016 because he could not think of anywhere else to put it and could not throw it away.
She has stood in front of that drawer four times.

2017. March. Eleven o'clock in the morning on a Tuesday. She got as far as putting her hand on the handle and then went downstairs and got in the car and drove to Ballyholme and swam for two hours in eight-degree water, which was forty minutes longer than was safe, and Sadie was not there and there was nobody on the beach and she has never told anybody how long she was in.

2019. The night before the Robben Island swim, in a hotel in Cape Town, which is to say she stood in front of a drawer that was nine thousand kilometres away, in her head, for about forty minutes, and then went down to the bar and had a glass of wine, which she does not do.

2021. December. She opened it. She got the envelope out. She held it for some period of time and put it back and closed the drawer, and went and sat on the stairs, and Dariush found her there at about one in the morning and sat down two steps below her and did not say anything, and after twenty minutes she said, "It's not that I don't want to know."
And he said, "I know."
And she said, "It's that once I've read it, that's it. That's the last thing. There isn't anything after it."
And he said — and this was one of the four or five times in ten years that he came close, and she has thought about it a great deal since —
"Farangis, there isn't anything in it."
And she said, "Then why did you put it under a dishwasher manual?"
2024. She did not open it. She stood in the doorway of the back bedroom for a while with the light off and then went to bed.
Here is the shape of the ten years, and it is not the shape people imagine, and the difference matters.

The first year was volume. Eighty kilometres a week, which is more than any sane build, and which everybody around her called grief and approved of. She did not miss a day. She was, that year, the most disciplined she has ever been about anything, and the discipline had nothing whatever to do with strength, and she has said so once, to the woman in Belfast, who wrote it down.

The second year was the anger, and the anger was entirely misdirected, by design. She fell out with the club. She fell out with a woman called Ann over the arrangement of a gala. She fell out, spectacularly and permanently, with a journalist from a Sunday paper who wanted to write about her and who used, in an email, the phrase in the wake of the tragedy, and who received four hundred words in reply that she has never regretted and would not send now.
The third and fourth years were the house.

That is the part that is not discussed. There is a room, and the room is a nineteen-year-old's room, and there is a schedule of decisions to be made about it that nobody schedules and that arrives anyway. What comes off the walls and when. Whether the wardrobe is emptied in an afternoon or over four years, one bag at a time, which is what actually happens. Which of his things become objects that live in the house — the good ones, the ones you can put on a shelf — and which of them become the other kind, the ones that cannot be looked at and cannot be got rid of and therefore go into a box in the roof space, and the box in the roof space is the truest thing in the house and nobody ever opens it.

There is a specific, unbearable, entirely unmentionable category of object which is: the ordinary thing that is worth nothing and was touched daily. A phone charger. A bank card. A blue plastic comb from a chemist's, still with hair in it, discovered in a coat in the hall in February 2018, which stopped Farangis Roshanfar entirely for eleven minutes.
The fifth year she went to the woman in Belfast, and it helped, substantially, and permanently, and she stopped going in the eleventh month because the woman wanted to work on the seconds.
The sixth year she went back to the channels properly and did Tsugaru at the fourth attempt.

The seventh, eighth and ninth years she trained, and worked in a school office, and made dinner, and slept next to her husband, and swam forty times a year in cold water with her face down, and was, by any external measure, entirely recovered, and was in fact conducting a ten-year legal action in an empty room against a defendant who was herself, with no judge, no jury, no charge, no evidence, and no possibility of any finding whatsoever.
And in the tenth year she booked the North Channel and rang the association and asked, by name, for an observer.

Dariush found out in March. She had not told him. He found the email open on the laptop in the kitchen — genuinely by accident, he was looking for a boarding pass — and he read the name and stood in the kitchen for a while with the laptop open.
He did not say anything about it that day, or that month.
He said something about it in June, in the car, coming back from Strangford after the qualifier, with her hair still wet and the heater off, forty minutes into a fifty-minute drive.
He said: "Why Ailbhe."
And she said: "Because she was on the rail."
And he said: "Farangis. She's been on that rail for ten years."
And she looked out of the window at the Ards peninsula going past in the rain and said: "Then it's time somebody let her off it."

Which was, Dariush thought, the single most generous sentence she had produced in a decade, and also — and he could not have said this to her, and would not have been able to say it to anybody, and knew it with total certainty — completely and entirely a lie about her own motives, and he loved her enough not to ask her which of the two of them she thought she was rescuing.
Feed Twenty-One
At 12:00, at the twenty-first feed, ten hours in, Farangis stopped treading and put her feet down into nothing and shouted across four metres of water at a woman with a clipboard.
"Ailbhe."
Nobody moved on the boat. Dariush stood with the pole and the empty bottle on the end of it.
"Ailbhe!"
Ailbhe Nunan came to the rail.
"You're wasting a feed," she said.
"Did he say anything."
The engine ran. The boat rose and fell about a foot.
"Farangis, get your head down."

"You were the only one who could hear. Dariush was in the water, Marek was steering, the other lad was on the light." Her voice came in pieces because she was breathing hard and shipping water and shouting, all at once, which is not a thing the human throat is designed to do. "You were on the rail with the sheet. Twelve feet. You were the only one in a position to hear anything. Did he say anything."
Ailbhe Nunan stood at the rail of the Kestrel Star with her clipboard against her chest.
"I'm the observer," she said.
"I know what you are."

"Then you know what I do and what I don't do." She said it without heat and without apology. "I'm not going to have a conversation with you at hour ten. You've twenty hours in front of you. I'm not putting anything into your head that has to sit in there for twenty hours."
"That's not a no."
"It's not a yes."
"Ailbhe—"
"Ask me in Portpatrick."
Farangis Roshanfar hung in the water for three seconds with her goggles up on her forehead.
Then she put them down, and put her face in, and went.
Ailbhe went back to the seat under the wheelhouse and sat down and wrote:
12:00. Feed 21. 41 seconds — swimmer stationary, addressing observer. All taken. Water 12.2. Air 17. Sea state 2. Stroke rate on resumption 59. Condition: good.

Forty-one seconds. It was the longest feed of the swim so far by nineteen seconds and it had cost her, at two and a half kilometres an hour with a knot of ebb under her, something in the region of forty metres.
Dariush pulled the line in and stowed the bottle and came and stood near her, not looking at her, watching the water.
"She's going to ask you again," he said.
"I know."

"She's going to ask you at three in the morning when she's got a core of thirty-four and she's fifteen hours in and she'll be able to make herself cry, which she can't do now, and you'll be tired too."
"I know."

"I'm telling you as the only other person who was on that boat," said Dariush, still watching the water, "that if you tell her anything before she's on the shingle, she will not finish. Not because she'll be upset. Because she'll stop needing to."
Ailbhe Nunan wrote the air temperature in a box on a form.
"I know that as well," she said.
Hour Fourteen
The afternoon is the part nobody writes about, because there is nothing in it, and that is precisely the thing.

From about ten in the morning until about seven in the evening the North Channel on a good day in August is a wide, bright, blank, entirely benign expanse of grey-green water under a high sky, with the Irish coast gone behind and the Scottish coast a low line that does not appear to get any closer for six hours because it genuinely does not get any closer for six hours, because she is crossing a tide that is running sideways at more than her own speed.

Air seventeen. Water twelve point two. Wind under five knots. Sea state one, occasionally two. Gannets. A ferry, twice, four kilometres to the north, going somewhere with a bar in it. One basking shark at 13:40, three metres of it, which Dessie pointed out and which Farangis never saw and was not told about until Portpatrick.
Perfect conditions. The kind of day a swimmer waits four years for.
And it is the worst part of the swim, and every experienced marathon swimmer will tell you so, and none of them can explain it to anyone who has not done it.

Because the storm has a shape. Cold has a shape. Jellyfish have a shape. Pain, nausea, a headwind, a tide that turns early — these are events, and events can be swum through, and a swimmer's entire architecture is built for swimming through events.
There is no architecture for nothing at all.

At hour twelve she had done approximately forty-three thousand strokes. Every one of them identical. The visual field had not changed in twelve hours except for the light going from black to grey to blue. She had heard nothing but her own breathing and an engine. She had eaten twenty-four bottles of the same drink.
And there were eighteen hours left.

This is where the technique is actually spent. Not in the dark, not in the field — here, at two in the afternoon, in the sunshine, in the flat, with a boat alongside and a husband on the rail and nothing whatsoever wrong.

The mind, denied all input, does what it always does, which is to go looking for the largest available object, and the largest available object is the total remaining distance, and the total remaining distance at hour twelve is eighteen hours of this.
The technique says: you are not swimming eighteen hours. You are swimming to the feed. There are twenty-three minutes.
And the mind, which has been in the small room for twelve hours and is bored, says: twenty-three minutes of what, though.

She lost it at 14:20 for the first time in the swim, properly, the way you lose it — not panic, nothing dramatic, simply a collapse of the partition, and for about ninety seconds Farangis Roshanfar swam the whole North Channel at once, saw all of it, the eighteen hours, the dark that was coming, the field, the last two kilometres, and the entire distance stood up in front of her like a wall and her stroke rate went from fifty-eight to sixty-six, which is the signature, which is what it looks like from a boat.
Dariush saw it from the rail and did not say anything, because there is nothing to say, and because a feeder who addresses it makes it worse by confirming that it is visible.

She got it back at about 14:24. She got it back by doing the thing she had been taught by nobody and had worked out for herself in the Bristol Channel in 2014, which was to stop counting to four hundred and start counting to twenty.

Twenty strokes. That is the smallest room. When four hundred is too big — and at some point in every long swim four hundred becomes too big — you go to twenty, and twenty is about twenty-one seconds, and there is nothing in twenty-one seconds. Nothing can go wrong in it. No decision is required in it. You can hold twenty for eighteen hours if you have to, one at a time, and there are three thousand and eighty-six of them, and you do not count those.
She did twenty-stroke sets from 14:24 until 15:10.
At 15:00, feed twenty-seven, she said: "Talk to me."
Which is the standard request and every feeder has a repertoire and the repertoire is the most carefully constructed thing on the boat.
The rules of feeder talk, developed by Dariush Roshanfar over twenty-five years and never written down:
Nothing that requires an answer. She has one breath and it is not for conversation.
Nothing about time remaining, ever, unless she asks directly, and then round.
Nothing about how well she is doing, because it invites her to check, and checking is fatal.
Nothing about home. Nothing about anything with feeling in it. A swimmer at hour fourteen has no defences whatsoever and a sentence about a kitchen will put her in the kitchen for forty minutes.
Nothing new. Nothing she has to think about.
What is left, after all that, is a very narrow and very strange category, which is: absolutely trivial, entirely familiar, mildly irritating information.
So he told her about the boiler.

He told her, in instalments, over four feeds, about the ongoing dispute with the man who had come to service the boiler in Bangor in May and had said the expansion vessel needed replacing and had quoted four hundred and ten pounds, and about the second man, who had come in June, and had said the vessel was fine, and about what the first man had said when Dariush rang him about it, and about the review Dariush had drafted and not posted, and about the specific wording of the review, which had gone through several versions.

It is one of the stupidest conversations either of them ever had and it took forty-five minutes across four feeds and she asked, at feed thirty, unprompted, what the second man had charged for the callout, and Dariush knew at that moment that she had come back and would be all right until dark.
At 16:00 the tide slackened and turned and began to carry her north again and Wilson altered course eleven degrees and said nothing to anybody about it.
At 17:30 she asked the time and he rounded down by twelve minutes.

At 18:40 a pod of common dolphins came through, eight or nine of them, and stayed with the boat for about four minutes, and one of them came under her twice, close enough that she felt the pressure wave, and she stopped and lifted her head and watched them go, and for the first time since Donaghadee she laughed out loud in the water, and it sounded, from the deck, like something breaking.
"Feed's early," said Dariush, sending it out at 18:44.
"I'm not due."
"You're due. Take it."
She took it.
"Dariush."
"What."
"That was the best thing that's ever happened to me," said Farangis Roshanfar, at hour sixteen and forty-four minutes, in the North Channel, entirely seriously, and put her face down and swam.
Hour Nineteen

The light went at 21:30, which is late in early August at that latitude, and it went the way it goes over water on a clear evening, which is slowly and then all at once: a long orange hour with the swell picking it up in slabs, then twenty minutes of a green-grey in which the surface still had a shine on it, then nothing.

At 21:00, feed thirty-nine, Dariush cracked the first of the glow sticks and clipped it to the back of her goggle strap between the shoulder blades, using the pole, which took four attempts because it has to be clipped and not handed and neither party may touch the other. He had done it seven hundred times and it had never once gone smoothly.
The lamps went on at 21:40 and the world contracted to the size of a lit room again.
Nineteen and a half hours.

She had, by Wilson's reckoning, done just over twenty-one kilometres over the ground and had thirteen and a half left, and the second ebb had begun and was going to run until half past midnight, and after that there was a flood which would take her north and then a slack around six in the morning, and if she was where Wilson wanted her at six she would be on the Scottish coast in the middle of the morning.
If she was not, she would be swimming in the afternoon, into a wind that was forecast to come round westerly at force four by two.
At the last feed of the light she said: "How long."
"Nineteen hours."
"How long left."
"That depends on you."
"How long, Dariush."
"Eleven or twelve. Maybe more."
She took the bottle. She had to think about the release for the first time.
"Farangis."
She was already turning away.

"It's going to get dark now," he said, "and it's going to be dark for a long time, and you're going to see things. You know you are. You always do and this is a long one and you're going to see things earlier and see more of them."
"I know what happens."

"I'm saying it out loud so it's been said out loud." His voice went across three metres of water flatly, without any particular tenderness, in the manner of a man reading out a checklist, which was the only manner in which either of them could ever say anything that counted. "They're not real. All of it's not real. And it doesn't matter that it's not real, you don't have to fight it, you don't have to argue with it. You just have to keep your hand going in at eleven o'clock."
The boat rose. The last of the green went off the water.
"And if you see anything," said Dariush, "on the left."
She waited.

"On the left," he said again, and stopped, because he had started a sentence he did not know the end of, and had known he did not know the end of it, and had started it anyway, which was the most reckless thing he had done in ten years.
Farangis Roshanfar trod water in the North Channel in the dark with a green glow stick on her back.
"Say it," she said.
"Take the whole bottle," said Dariush.
She put her face in the water and swam.
PART THREE — THE FIELD
The Dark
Here is what there is.

There is a green light on your own back that you cannot see and that exists entirely for other people. There is a boat on the left with two lamps angled down, and the lamps make a cone in the water about four metres across, and inside the cone the sea is a lit brown-green and outside the cone it is nothing at all, and the boundary between them travels with you at your exact speed for hours.

There is your right hand entering the water at eleven o'clock. You can see it. It is the only object in the universe that you can see and that is yours. It is greyish and it is slightly wrong, and it goes in and pushes a stream of small silver bubbles down its length and the bubbles come off the fingers and roll back along the arm and past the shoulder and go, and then it is not there any more, and then there is the left arm, which you cannot see, because you are breathing on the left and your face is out of the water when the left arm works.

There is the sound, which is not silence. It is a very loud, very consistent white noise made of your own breathing amplified through bone, the boil of water at your ears, the boat's engine at fifteen hundred revs coming through the water rather than the air, and the sixty-times-a-minute percussion of your own hands. It is roughly as loud as a busy road. Swimmers who have never done a night swim expect silence and find instead that they are inside a machine.
There is the smell of nothing, because there is no smell.

There is the taste, which is salt and maltodextrin and, from about hour fifteen, blood, because the salt has been working on the inside of your lips and the corners of your mouth for a day and there is a split there now.

There is the temperature, which is twelve point two, and which you stopped experiencing as temperature about eighteen hours ago and now experience as a kind of ambient pressure, a fact about the world rather than a sensation in the body.
And there is the count.

That is the entire contents of the mind of a marathon swimmer at hour twenty-one, and it is worth pausing on how extraordinarily little that is, because it is the whole mechanism of everything that follows.

The technical term is sensory deprivation and it is not a metaphor. Every channel is a flotation tank with weather. The visual field is a repeating loop of four seconds' duration. The auditory field is broadband noise with no information in it. The proprioceptive field is one movement pattern executed a hundred thousand times. Temperature is constant. There is no smell, no taste that changes, no social input, no language, no decisions to make.

The brain is a prediction engine. That is all it is. It exists to build a model of the world and to check the model against the incoming data and to update the model where it is wrong. Take away the data — properly take it away, for a day — and it does not stop. It cannot stop. It goes on producing the model at full power with nothing to correct it, and what you get, reliably, in every human being who has ever been in this condition, are perceptions built out of pure prediction with no evidence in them at all.

The literature is unambiguous and it is oddly beautiful. Prisoners in solitary. Polar explorers. Solo sailors. Pilots at altitude in the 1950s. High-altitude climbers above eight thousand metres. And swimmers, who get it worse than almost anybody, because the swimmer combines sensory poverty with hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, and a day and a half without sleep.

They report: light where there is no light. Music, often orchestral, often specific. Buildings on the water. Conversations with crew that the crew did not have and can prove they did not have, because they were asleep, because they were on the other side of the boat, because they were dead. Roads. The certainty of being able to see the bottom, in three kilometres of water, in the dark, in perfect detail. Animals. Children.
And the third man: a companion, walking or climbing or swimming alongside, on the side away from the group, benign, silent, and absolutely convincing.

Shackleton had it crossing South Georgia and put it in the book and gave it the name. Every high-altitude mountaineer knows it. It is so consistent across cultures and centuries that there is a decent argument that it is not a malfunction at all but a specific, evolved, last-resort response of a social animal in extremis, which produces a companion because a companion is what keeps you moving, and which has therefore been selected for over a very long time, in exactly the conditions in which a solitary human being would otherwise lie down.
Farangis knew all of this. She had read the papers. She had read them in the way that a person reads about a country they intend to enter.
At 23:00, feed forty-three, twenty-one hours in, she took the bottle and said:
"It's started."
"What has," said Dariush.
"There's an orchestra."
"Right."
"It's not even good."
"What is it."
"It's the Ulster Orchestra doing something with a lot of brass in it and I don't like brass," said Farangis, and let the bottle go, and put her face down, and swam.

Dariush pulled the line in, and wrote 23:00 — auditory, benign, insight intact, and then stood at the rail for a while, watching the green light going away from him and coming back, going away and coming back, in the cone of the lamps.

Insight intact. That is the phrase and it is the whole game. A hallucination with insight is a curiosity: you see the thing, you know it is not there, you carry on. A hallucination without insight is a woman at hour twenty-six climbing a staircase that is not there, which has happened, and which is how people drown three metres from a boat.
The clinical question is not is she seeing things. Everybody sees things. The clinical question is does she still know.
Lion's Mane
They came into the field at 23:40 and it lasted, on and off, for six hours.

Every channel has a signature and this is the North Channel's, and it is the reason that a crossing which is only thirty-four and a half kilometres — shorter than the Molokai, barely longer than the English — has been completed by fewer than a hundred and thirty people. Not the cold, although the cold is worse than the English by a full three degrees. Not the tide, although the tide is worse. The Cyanea capillata. The lion's mane jellyfish. The largest jellyfish in the world, an animal of the cold north Atlantic that in that channel in August aggregates in numbers that have no equivalent anywhere else on a recognised marathon route.

The bell can be over a metre across. The tentacles — and this is the part that matters — trail for ten metres, fifteen, in some specimens more than thirty, in a fine dense curtain of hundreds of individual filaments, and they are almost invisible in daylight and entirely invisible at night, and they extend far below and far around the animal, so that the swimmer who sees the bell and swims around it has, by seeing the bell, already been in the tentacles for eight metres.

There is no avoiding them. That is the first thing every North Channel aspirant is told and it is not a warning, it is a scheduling note. You do not avoid the field, you swim through the field, and it is six hours long, and it is in the dark.

The sting is a nematocyst discharge: hundreds of thousands of microscopic barbed capsules, each pressurised, each firing on contact, injecting a mixed venom into the epidermis. Contact with human skin is not a bite or a burn but an injection performed by an organism that does not know you are there and has no opinion about you.
What it does at first is nothing. There is a lag of two or three seconds and swimmers say this is the worst part, because you know precisely what is arriving.
Then a line of fire.
The first one caught her across the back of the right hand and up the forearm at 23:41 and she said, aloud, into the water, a word she did not use.
The second was across the mouth.

That is the one they tell you about. Face and lips and — because you are breathing every two on the left with your mouth open — inside the mouth. The tongue. The soft palate. The inside of the cheek. Venom on mucous membrane rather than skin, where there is no keratin layer to slow it down, and the tissue responds by swelling, and there is a specific and entirely rational terror that goes with feeling the inside of your own throat begin to thicken twelve kilometres from land.
She kept swimming. There is nothing else. That is the entire content of the technique.
By midnight she had been hit eleven times and had stopped counting, which is a thing every North Channel swimmer does at about the same point.

By 01:00 the back of her neck, both shoulders, both forearms, the backs of both hands, her mouth, her chin, her left ear, and a long diagonal across the sternum that had gone in under the costume strap.

The crew could see nothing. That is the horror of it from the boat: in the lamps you get a flash of a bell now and then, a translucent brown-orange plate the size of a bin lid rolling under the surface, and you get the swimmer's rhythm breaking for two strokes, and that is all the information there is. Dessie, who had done eighty of these, kept up a running count of visible bells for Wilson, and the count between midnight and one was forty-one.

Under the rules there is nothing to be done. She could not be given anything. Nobody could put vinegar on her, or a compress, or a hand. Any topical treatment must be self-applied and there is no way to self-apply anything to your own back while treading water in the dark, and the standard practice — which every North Channel swimmer follows and which the association has never quite formally approved — is to take an antihistamine with a feed and continue.
At the 01:00 feed Dariush sent out the bottle and a second, smaller bottle with two tablets in it.
"Cetirizine and paracetamol," he said. "Take both."
She could not get the small bottle open.

She hung in the water in the dark with a green light on her back and worked at a child-proof cap with two hands that had stopped closing four hours previously, and Dariush stood at the rail with a pole in his hand at a distance of three metres and watched his wife fail to open a bottle of antihistamines for fifty-one seconds.
He could have done it in a second and a half.

That is the sport. That is the entire moral content of the sport in one image, and anybody who wants to understand why these people are the way they are should look at it for a while: a man with the tablet bottle open in his mind, and a rule, and three metres of black water, and fifty-one seconds.
She got it. She took both. She let go of both bottles and swam.
"Fifty-one seconds," said Dariush.
Ailbhe Nunan wrote 01:00. Feed 47. 51 seconds. Both taken. Extensive envenomation, ongoing. Swimmer did not request assistance.
And in the second column she wrote: Nobody offered any.
And she left it in.
At 02:00 they had been going twenty-four hours and Wilson came out of the wheelhouse for the first time since dark and stood beside Dariush and looked at the water for a long moment.
"She's up on the line," he said. "She'll do it if she holds."
"Will she hold."
"She's twenty-four hours in the North Channel with a face like that," said Wilson, "and she's still taking the whole bottle. I've had fellas in here at eight hours crying about a wasp."
He went back into the wheelhouse.
The Second Swimmer
It arrived at 01:20 and it arrived the way they always do, which is that it had been there for some time before she noticed it.

That is the thing the accounts get wrong when they are written up afterwards. Nobody sees a figure appear. The figure has been there, and at some point the swimmer becomes aware that she has been aware of it for a while, and the awareness comes with the entire history attached, so that there is no moment of onset to point at. It is a memory that arrives as a perception.
On her left. The side away from the boat.
About a metre and a half off her shoulder, slightly behind, in the black outside the cone of the lamps, where there was nothing to see and no light to see it by.
Swimming.

Breathing every two on the left, in phase with her, so that when she turned her head to breathe, the other head was turning too, out there in the dark, at the same instant, and had already turned, and was turning again.
Farangis Roshanfar swam four hundred strokes and did not look.

That is the discipline and she held it and it was one of the two or three hardest things she had ever done. Four hundred strokes, six minutes and fifty seconds at fifty-eight a minute, with something matching her stroke a metre and a half to port, and she did not lift her head, and she did not turn, and she went on putting her right hand in at eleven o'clock, because Dariush had said you just have to keep your hand going in at eleven o'clock, and it was the only instruction she had.

She had been here before. Twice. She knew the physiology. She could have given a lecture on it while it was happening and part of her was giving one: this is a hypothermic, hypoglycaemic, sleep-deprived, sensorily starved brain generating a social presence because that is what this brain does in this condition, it is Shackleton on the ridge, it is the mountaineer's fourth man, it is the most reliably reported perceptual event in the entire literature of human extremity, and it has a name, and it means nothing, and it is not him.
At the end of the four hundred she started again at one.
At two hundred and sixty she looked.

There was nothing there. Of course. Black water, a metre and a half of it, and the end of the light, and past that the North Channel going down two hundred metres to a bed of sand and shell that no one has ever seen.
She put her face down.

And the presence, which had not gone anywhere, and which had not been affected in the slightest by being looked at and found absent, went on swimming beside her, breathing every two on the left, in phase.
Here is what it is like, and this is the part that people who have not had it cannot be made to understand, and the part that people who have had it never argue about:
