It is not visual. She could not see him. She looked and there was nothing and looking made no difference at all, because the perception was not being generated in the visual system. It was being generated much deeper down, in whatever apparatus it is that tells a human animal, in a dark room, with its eyes closed, that there is somebody else in the room.

That apparatus does not report images. It reports presence. And it does not answer to evidence, because it evolved in a world where the cost of a false positive was a wasted turn of the head and the cost of a false negative was death.
So there was a person in the water on her left.
She knew there was not.

Both of these were completely true at the same time and neither of them was available to correct the other, and this is the actual condition, and it is not madness, and every account that reports it as madness was written by somebody who has not been at hour twenty-three.
At 01:30 the feed came out on the pole and she took it and drank and gave it back.
"How is it," said Dariush.
"Fine."
"Farangis."
"It's fine."

She let go of the bottle and turned and put her face in the water, and swam eleven strokes, and then stopped, and stood up in two hundred metres of water the way swimmers do, upright, treading, and turned back to the boat with her goggles still down.
"Dariush."
He was already pulling the line in. He stopped.
"What."
There was a long moment in which the boat rose and fell and the engine ran and the green light on her back went in and out of the water.
"How many people are in the water," said Farangis Roshanfar.
On the port side, under the wheelhouse, Ailbhe Nunan put down her pen.
"One," said Dariush.
"Right," said Farangis.
"Farangis. How many do you think there are."
"One," she said. "There's one. I know there's one."
And then, with a clarity that would come back to her a great many times in the following six hours, and which she would never be able to decide the meaning of, she said:
"I'm not asking because I don't know. I'm asking because I wanted to hear somebody say it."
She swam.
Dariush wrote 01:30 — asked how many swimmers in water. Insight intact. and then looked at what he had written and added, in smaller letters, (I think.)
Hour Twenty-Four
At 02:00 the presence began correcting her.

It did not speak. This needs saying plainly because the temptation to make it speak is enormous and the truth is stranger and much worse. It did not say anything. There was no voice. There was never at any point a voice.
What happened was that details arrived.

She was running the memory. She had been running the memory, in fragments, since about hour eighteen, without deciding to, the way you run a memory when the mind has nothing else to do and the doors have come off the rooms. September 2016. The English Channel, the return leg of a two-way, hour nineteen. The boat. The lights. Sohrab going in at the shoulder.
And at hour twenty-four in the North Channel, with something swimming beside her that was not there, the memory began to come with items in it that she did not put there.
The first was the cap.

In her memory of that night — the memory she had carried for ten years, examined ten thousand times, given evidence from, built a decade of self-accusation on — Sohrab was wearing a green cap. She could see it. Green, the club's colour, with the club's name on it.
At 02:04 in the North Channel it was orange.
Not a doubt. Not a suggestion. The memory simply presented itself, in its entirety, with an orange cap in it, in the way a memory presents itself, with the full weight of having always been that way.
She lost her stroke for four strokes.

Then she thought, coldly, with the part of her that was still an instrument: this is confabulation, this is a degraded brain rebuilding a file it cannot read, this is exactly what happens and I have read about it and I will not do this.
At 02:20 the water in the memory changed direction.

At 02:35 the number of people on the deck went from four to three, and she could not get it back to four, and she went through them one by one — Marek at the wheel, Ailbhe on the rail, the boy on the light, Dariush — and every time she counted them she got four, and every time she saw the deck she saw three.
At 02:50 she remembered, with complete clarity, that she had turned and looked at him at feed nineteen and that he had held up both hands with the fingers spread.
She had never remembered that before. Not once in ten years.

And this is the moment, at hour twenty-four, in the middle of the North Channel, that Farangis Roshanfar came apart, and it is worth being exact about the mechanism, because it is not what it looks like.
It looks like grief. It is not grief. Grief she could do; she had done ten years of it and had it in a system.

What was happening was epistemological, and it went like this: for a decade she had lived inside a single account of one night, and she had used that account as the foundation of everything — her guilt, her marriage, her not-reading of a document in a drawer, her presence in this channel — and she had believed, without ever examining the belief, that the account was a record.
And at hour twenty-four the account had begun to edit itself in front of her, freely, in real time, with no more difficulty than changing the colour of a hat.
Which meant it had always been able to do that.

Which meant it was not a record. It was a reconstruction, and it had been reconstructed every single time she had gone to it, ten thousand times over ten years, and each reconstruction had been laid down again on top of the last one, and what she had in her head now had approximately the relationship to September 2016 that a photocopy of a photocopy has to a face.
The thing she had been prosecuting herself with was not evidence.

The thing she had been prosecuting herself with was a story she had been telling herself nightly for ten years, in a state of extreme distress, which is precisely the condition under which the human memory is at its most plastic and its most confident.
She stopped swimming.
She had not stopped swimming outside a feed in eleven years.
"Farangis!"
The boat came round about ten degrees; Wilson had felt it before Dariush shouted.

She was upright in the water with her goggles up, and the green stick on her back was going in and out of the black, and the lion's mane welts across her mouth had swollen the lower lip out and to the left so that when she spoke it came out damaged.
"Dariush. Was his cap green."
"What?"
"Sohrab's cap. On the night. Was it green or orange."
Three metres of water. Twenty-four hours and four minutes. A man at a rail with a pole in his hand.
He could have said either. He knew what she was doing and he knew what it would cost her either way, and he had about a second and a half.
"It was green," he said.
"You're sure."
"It was the club cap. It was green. Farangis, swim."
"You'd say that anyway."
"I would," said Dariush, "and it's also true. Both of those are true. Swim."
She looked at him for two more seconds and then put her face down and swam, and her stroke rate on resumption was fifty-one, which was five below her last count, and Ailbhe Nunan wrote it down.
What She Thought
Now the rest of it.

This is the part that has no defence and is not going to be given one, and there is no useful purpose in arranging it kindly, so it will be set down in the order it arrived, at hour twenty-five, in the middle of the North Channel, in a woman who had been awake for forty-four hours and in twelve-degree water for twenty-five of them, with something swimming beside her that was not there.
One.

When they got him onto the deck she was still in the water. This is a fact and it is in every account including the two-line one. Under the rules she could not be lifted out except by abandoning, and the swim was not formally abandoned until Marek made the call, and there is therefore an interval — the length of it is disputed, nobody wrote it down, Dariush says ninety seconds and Ailbhe has never said — during which her son was on the deck and she was in the water beside the boat and Dariush was doing compressions.
And in that interval, treading water in the dark in the English Channel at hour nineteen of a two-way with her son's arm hanging off the edge of a deck three metres above her, she thought:
If they get him back I can still finish.

That is the first thing. There is no version of it that is not that. She has tried. She has tried the version where it is her body thinking it and not her. She has tried the version where it is a mother's optimism, the belief that he will be fine, and therefore innocent. She knows both of those are constructions and she built them herself and she knows exactly when.
The sentence was about the swim.
Two.
When Marek abandoned the swim — when the words were actually said, and the boat turned for Dover — the thing that went through her, before anything else, before terror, before any of it, was relief.

Because she had been in the water for nineteen hours and she was one hundred and ten hours away from being a woman who had swum the English Channel and back, and she had known since about hour sixteen, in the way you know these things, that she was not going to make it, and that she was going to have to abandon in front of her son.
And now she did not have to.

That is the second thing. The abandonment arrived as a release, and she felt the release, physically, in her chest, at three in the morning in the English Channel, over the sound of her husband counting compressions.
Three.
She wanted Dariush to hit her.
Not metaphorically, and not once, and not in the aftermath. Continuously, for ten years, as a standing wish, renewed almost daily and never once approached in speech.

She wanted him to come into a room and put a hand around her throat and say you killed him. She has staged it. She has an entire scene, with dialogue, which she has run so many times that it has acquired production values: the kitchen in Bangor, the light off, the specific chair.
The wish is not masochism. She has checked. It is procedural.

She wants a charge. A charge is the beginning of a process, and a process has a shape, and at the end of a shape there is a verdict, and after a verdict there is a sentence, and a sentence has a duration, and a duration ends.

Instead she got a man who loved her, who knew the physiology better than she did, who had run every number and had arrived, honestly, at there was nothing you could have done, and who said it, and went on saying it, kindly, for ten years.
Which meant no charge. Which meant no process. Which meant no end.

She has come to experience her husband's forgiveness as a locked door, and she has come, in the small hours, in the years since, to hate him for it — not steadily, not in a way that touches the marriage, but in short, complete, incandescent episodes lasting under a minute, in which she looks at the back of his head while he is asleep and thinks: you coward, say it.
Four.
The body.

In the fourteen months after Sohrab died she trained more than she has ever trained in her life. Eighty kilometres a week. Two sessions a day, sometimes three. Everybody around her called it grief and told each other, approvingly, that she was coping, and she let them.
And what she has never said to a single living person is what the body did in those months, which is that it woke up.

Twice a day she went into cold water and half killed herself and came out with a nervous system flooded with catecholamines and endorphins and every endogenous opioid a mammal can produce, and the effect was not calm. The effect was appetite. She was, at thirty-seven, four months after burying her son, more physically alive than she had been at twenty-five: hungry, wakeful, and — she is going to say it — aroused, persistently, absurdly, in the middle of the afternoon, in the car, in the kitchen, in a house with a photograph of a boy in the hall.
And she took it. She used it. She initiated, more in that year than in the previous five, with a man who was destroyed and who did not understand what was happening and who did not refuse her.
And afterwards she would lie in the dark next to him and feel the whole system come down off it, and would think, in her own voice, with perfect clarity: what kind of animal is this.

She has never told him. He has never asked. It is the single largest unspoken thing in a marriage that has three or four large unspoken things in it, and it will still be unspoken when one of them dies, and both of them know that.
Five.
And under all of it, the thing that arrived last, at hour twenty-five, in the North Channel, with the presence swimming beside her in the dark:
She has not, in ten years, been able to remember what his voice sounded like.

She has the wet hand on her jaw at six years old, available on demand. She has the fingers spread in a gallery in 2011. She has the shape of him going into the water. She has, apparently, a green cap, or an orange one.

She does not have the voice. It went first and it went completely and it is not coming back, and she has an eleven-second video from 2015 of him in a kitchen saying something about a charger, and she has watched it perhaps four hundred times, and it has done what watching does, which is to overwrite the original with the copy, so that what she now has is not her son's voice but the sound of a phone speaker.
She destroyed it herself. By going to it.
That is what she thought at hour twenty-five, in the order she thought it.

And then she went on swimming, because there was nothing else to do with any of it, and because the water at that particular moment was the only place in the world that would take it, and because it was twelve point two degrees and it did not care, and because that is what the water has always been for.
The presence swam beside her in the dark.

At 03:00 the feed came out on the pole and she drank it and gave it back and said nothing at all, and Ailbhe Nunan wrote 03:00. Feed 51. 24 seconds. All taken. Condition: fair, and then sat with the pen above the second column for a long time, and did not write anything in it, and looked out at the water where a woman she had watched for twenty-five hours was swimming with her face down and her hand going in at eleven o'clock.
Hour Twenty-Six
At 04:00 she turned away from the bottle.

It is worth understanding what has happened by hour twenty-six to the machinery that makes decisions, because from here on the woman in the water is not the woman who got in, and the difference is chemical and structural and entirely predictable, and everybody on that boat had been waiting for it since the day before.

Blood glucose. She had taken eighty grams of carbohydrate an hour for twenty-six hours, which is close to the ceiling of what a human gut can absorb, and had burned somewhere between seven and eight hundred kilocalories an hour, so the deficit had been running at about four hundred an hour since the beginning and the arithmetic had now arrived. Liver glycogen: gone, hours ago. Muscle glycogen: gone in the prime movers, so the shoulders were running on fat oxidation and circulating glucose, and fat oxidation is slow and cannot support the intensity, and circulating glucose is what the brain eats.

And the brain does not have a store. It has about four grams of glucose in the whole bloodstream and it goes through that in a couple of minutes. It is entirely dependent on continuous delivery and when delivery drops it does not shut down evenly. It shuts down in order, and the order is: the newest parts first.
So the frontal lobe goes first. Judgment. Planning. Inhibition. The capacity to hold two things in mind and compare them. The capacity to be talked out of something.

Then the temperature. Core down, by Dariush's estimate — nobody was going to take a rectal temperature in the North Channel — somewhere around thirty-four point five, possibly a little under. At thirty-four the same structures are being suppressed by a different mechanism: enzyme kinetics slow, cerebral metabolism drops about six per cent per degree, and the effect is indistinguishable from the inside.
Two independent processes, both attacking the same organ, both taking out the same faculty first.
The result is a swimmer who is entirely lucid in the way that matters least — she can talk, she can count, she can swim — and who has lost, completely, the ability to be reasoned with.
"Take the bottle," said Dariush.
She turned her head away from it.

Not a refusal. Not a decision. A turn of the head, the way a child turns away from a spoon, and the whole of her body language was a child's and everybody on the deck recognised it and nobody said so.
"Farangis. Take the bottle."
"I don't want it."
"I know you don't want it. Take it."
"It makes me sick."
"It doesn't make you sick, you've had fifty-one of them."
"I don't want it."
Dessie held the light. Ryan the nephew stood at the rail with his mouth slightly open. Ailbhe Nunan wrote the time.

Here is the thing about the twenty-sixth hour, and every experienced feeder on every channel in the world knows it and dreads it: this is the exact and only mechanism by which competent, insulated, well-trained swimmers die on marathon crossings. Not the cold, on its own. Not the sea. The refusal cascade. She turns away from a feed. The glucose drops further. The judgment degrades further. She turns away from the next one. Twenty minutes later she cannot hold a stroke, and forty minutes after that she is at thirty-three degrees and going quiet, and the entire cascade began with a woman turning her head away from a bottle in a way that looked, at the time, like a small thing.
Two feeds missed is a swim. Three is a helicopter.
Dariush Roshanfar leaned over the rail of the Kestrel Star and shouted at his wife.
"Take the bottle!"
"Don't shout at me."
"Take the fucking bottle, Farangis."
"Don't—"

"You told me to. In the kitchen. On Tuesday. You said if you turn away from it twice I'm to shout at you and you'll think I'm a bully and I'm to keep doing it. That was you. You said it. So take the bottle."

She hung in the water with her ruined mouth and her hands that would not close and something swimming beside her that was not there, and for about four seconds she was, visibly, twelve years old and being got out of a bed.
Then she took the bottle.
She drank about half of it and gave it back.
"All of it."
"I drank it."
"You drank half."
"Dariush."
"All of it."
And she said — and this is the sentence that Dariush Roshanfar will still be able to reproduce exactly, with the intonation, when he is eighty:
"If I take all of it I'll finish."
The boat rose and fell.
"Yes," he said.
"I don't want to finish."
"I know."
"I want to stay out here."
"I know," said Dariush. "Take the whole bottle."
She took the whole bottle.
Ailbhe Nunan wrote: 04:00. Feed 53. 3 min 20 sec. Initial refusal. All taken after 2 min. Water 12.2. Air 13. Stroke rate on resumption 49. Condition: deteriorating.
And in the second column she wrote: Swimmer stated she did not wish to finish. Feeder instructed her to take the feed. She took it.
Eleven Seconds
At 04:40, in the last of the dark, it came.

Not as a memory. She would want to be clear about that afterwards, and she would never be able to make anybody understand it, including Dariush, including a woman in Belfast whom she would eventually go back to. It did not arrive as a memory. It arrived as a place.
She was in the English Channel.

Not remembering it. In it. The water changed under her — English Channel water is different water, warmer by three degrees, dirtier, and it tastes of shipping — and the boat on her left was a different boat, and the sky had a moon in it that had not been there in the North Channel, and she was nineteen hours into a two-way and she was going to have to abandon and she had not admitted it yet.
Hour nineteen. Feed nineteen. She had done nineteen hours and forty minutes and she was two hours off the English side on the return and her stroke had gone and she knew it.

Sohrab had been in the water since hour eighteen. One hour in three. He was on her left, a metre off, breathing every two on the left so that they were face to face on every second stroke, which was not standard, which was a thing he had started doing at about hour eighteen and forty and which she had not told him to stop doing because she liked it.
Green cap.
Orange cap.
Green.

The last time she saw him he was a body-length back and to the left and his arm came over and went in and she saw the whole of the stroke and it was good, it was a good stroke, his catch was better than hers had been at nineteen, and she had thought — and this she is sure of, this one she will defend, this one is hers — she had thought: look at that.
And then she swam eleven strokes.
And then she stopped.
Here is the hole. Here is the thing she has been swimming towards for ten years.

She stopped. She does not know why she stopped. She has, over a decade, produced a range of accounts of why she stopped, and she has believed all of them at different times, and the fact that she has produced a range is itself the problem.
Account one: she heard something. A sound behind her and to the left, in the water, that was not the rhythm.

Account two: she did not hear anything. She stopped because she was nineteen hours in and finished and her stroke had gone, and she stopped for the reason swimmers stop, which is that they cannot do it any more, and the timing is a coincidence, and the universe is full of coincidences and this one has ruined her life.

Account three, which arrives at three in the morning and which she has never told anybody: she heard something, and she knew what it was, and she stopped, and then she did not shout, and then she started swimming again, because she was two hours off the English coast on a two-way that she had already lost and because for eleven seconds she was not a mother, she was a system that had been running for nineteen hours with one objective in it.
She trod water for eleven seconds.

Eleven. That is Ailbhe's number, from the log, from the sheet, and Dariush has it too because Dariush counted it afterwards from the boat's engine note — eleven seconds between the swimmer stopping and the boat's screw going into reverse, and the boat's screw went into reverse because Ailbhe Nunan said, quite calmly, "Marek."

So: eleven seconds. Farangis Roshanfar stationary in the water. And then the boat turning, and Dariush going over the side in his clothes, and the light swinging, and everything after that is well documented and none of it matters, because the entire mass of a decade is loaded onto eleven seconds in which the only witness who could say what happened was the woman it happened to, and she does not know.
She did not shout. That is agreed. Nobody on the boat heard her shout, and Ailbhe was twelve feet away on the rail with a clipboard, and Ailbhe would have heard.
She has never been able to establish whether she did not shout because there was nothing to shout about, or because she was too cold to make a sound, or because she was in the process of deciding.
That is the hole, and it is eleven seconds wide, and she has been trying to get back into it for ten years by the only route she knows, which is to reproduce the conditions.

At 04:41 in the North Channel, at hour twenty-six and forty-one minutes, in the same cold, at the same hour of the night, at the same depth of the same exhaustion, with the same presence swimming beside her, Farangis Roshanfar went back in.

And she got there. She got all the way in. She was in the English Channel in September 2016 at the moment of stopping, with the whole of her nervous system in the correct state, and she looked, and this is what she found:
Nothing.

There was nothing there. There was no recovered memory, no sound, no decision, no revelation. There were eleven seconds of a woman treading water in the dark, and inside them there was no content at all, because there had never been any content, because the brain at hour nineteen and thirty-four point eight degrees does not lay down memory, full stop, and there is no key that opens a door with no room behind it.
She had built a ten-year religion on the assumption that the answer was in there.
There was no in there.
At 04:50 the sky over Scotland went from black to very dark blue with no event in between.
Dover

This is the part she has never been able to put in order, and it will be set down here in the order she has it, which is not the order it happened, because there is no order it happened, because the woman it happened to had a core temperature of thirty-four point one and was in the eighth hour of a hypoglycaemic episode and does not have the file.
The deck.

Wood under her cheek. Not the deck — a folded coat, and under the coat the deck, and the deck was going up and down, and the engine was much louder than it had been all night because she was lying on it.

Her legs would not do anything. That is not a memory of pain. It is a memory of an administrative problem: she gave an instruction and the instruction went nowhere, and she gave it again, with more emphasis, and it went nowhere again, and she remembers being irritated.
Somebody's knees beside her head.
A voice saying a number, over and over, in a rhythm, and the rhythm was familiar, and she could not place it, and it was the count.
Light swinging. The deck light on a lead, swinging, so the shadows went one way and then the other, and she remembers the shadows and not the thing casting them.
The face.

A woman's face upside down over hers, close, and grey hair coming out from under a hood, and a hand putting something heavy on her, and she remembers that the woman's face was doing something very carefully controlled, and that she recognised the control before she recognised the face.
What she said.
Here is what she has. She has this and it is all she has and she has taken it out and looked at it ten thousand times, which is to say she has ruined it:
She said, "Where's Sohrab."

She is certain of it. She said it first. That is the first thing out of her mouth on that deck, and she has said so in every account she has ever given, to Dariush, to the woman in Belfast, to her own head at four in the morning, and she believes it with the full force of a decade of daily repetition, and she now knows exactly what a decade of daily repetition is worth.
And the woman with the grey hair said something about them working on him.
And she tried to get up.
And that is the whole of it. That is the complete contents of the file. There is a hole after it that runs, as far as anybody can establish, about six hours.
Dover.
She was in a bed in a room with the curtain half round and it was daylight.

The first thing was that she was warm, and she noticed being warm before she noticed anything else, and the warmth was actively pleasant, and she lay in it for what she thinks was some time. Then she noticed her hands were bandaged, which they were not — they were not bandaged, they were just her hands, and she had misread them, and she remembers correcting it.
Then she thought: the swim.
Then she thought: I got out.
Then she thought, with a clean, procedural, entirely undramatic feeling of failure that she has never been able to make sound as small as it was: so I didn't finish, then.
And she lay in a bed in a hospital in Dover for some interval and was disappointed about a swim.

That is the fifth thing. That is the one that is not in the log and not in any account and that she has told nobody, including the woman in Belfast, and which arrived at hour twenty-five in the North Channel with the rest of it.

For an interval whose length is unknown — she thinks under a minute; she cannot swear to that; it might have been twenty seconds and it might have been five minutes — Farangis Roshanfar lay awake in a hospital bed in Kent and did not know, and was thinking about a swim.
Then Dariush came in.

He was in different clothes. That is what she saw first. He was in a grey sweatshirt that she did not recognise and that she later found out had been bought by somebody in a shop near the harbour, and the fact of the sweatshirt is the thing that has stayed, because it meant that time had passed and that arrangements had been made and that there had been a period in which people had gone into shops.
He came and sat down on the edge of the bed.
And she looked at his face and she knew.

There is a folk idea that people are told these things and cannot take them in, and it is wrong, and everybody who has been on either side of it knows it is wrong. She took it in instantly and completely, before a single word, from the arrangement of a man's face in a doorway, and everything that was said afterwards was administration.
He said her name.
She said, "No."
He said, "Farangis—"

She said, "No. No. No—" and went on saying it, and she does not know for how long, and it is the only part of that day for which she does not have a duration, and Dariush has never given her one, and she has never asked.
He held her.

That is the last thing in the file and it is a physical sensation and it is entirely intact, unlike everything around it: the weight of a man's hands flat between her shoulder blades, and the smell of a sweatshirt that had been in a shop that morning, and — because a body does not stop being a body, and because she had been in sixteen-degree water for nineteen hours and twelve minutes and had been out of it for eleven hours — the deep, involuntary, uncontrollable afterdrop shiver going through her the whole time, so that the two events are welded together and cannot be separated and never will be.
She has never in ten years been able to shiver without some part of it arriving.

Which is worth stating plainly, because it is the whole of what her life became: she had chosen, at eleven years old, on a beach in County Down, an activity whose central and unavoidable physical sensation is the exact sensation of being told her son was dead.
And she had gone on doing it, forty times a year, for ten years.
Nobody has ever asked her about that. It is too large and too obvious and it sits in the middle of her like a piece of furniture in a room that everybody walks around.
Hour Twenty-Eight
At 06:00 she got warm.

It came on over about ten minutes and it was the most pleasant sensation she had experienced in a day and a half. It began in the chest and went out along the arms, and it was not the false warmth of a hot drink or the local warmth of effort; it was general, it was deep, and it was accompanied by a flooding, generous, entirely convincing sense of wellbeing.
The welts stopped hurting.
Her hands, which had been paddles since midnight, felt like hands.

The stroke felt long and easy and correct in a way it had not felt since hour four, and when she looked at her own arm entering the water it looked, in the grey first light, like a young woman's arm, and she thought: there we are. That's the second wind. Everybody talks about it.
She had been swimming for twenty-eight hours and she was four kilometres off the Scottish coast and she felt marvellous.

Paradoxical warmth. Paradoxical undressing. It is one of the most reliably reported findings in hypothermia medicine and one of the most reliably fatal. Somewhere below thirty-three degrees, after hours of maximal vasoconstriction, the smooth muscle in the peripheral arterioles fatigues and lets go, and a large volume of warm core blood rushes out to the shell. The receptors in the skin, which have been reporting cold for a day, are suddenly bathed in blood at core temperature and report — accurately, from their point of view — heat.
The subjective experience is warmth and comfort and, very often, euphoria.
The physiological reality is that the core has just been opened to the environment and is about to fall off a cliff.

They find them on mountains with their coats off and their boots beside them. They find them in flats in January in a vest. Between twenty and fifty per cent of fatal hypothermia cases involve the removal of clothing, by the victim, at the point of death, because the victim was hot.
At 06:08 Farangis Roshanfar reached up with her right hand and put a thumb under the strap of her costume at the left shoulder.
It was Dessie who saw it and Dessie who said, sharply, "Boss."
Dariush was already at the rail.
"Farangis."

She had stopped swimming. She was treading, easily, comfortably, with her head up and her goggles pushed onto her forehead, and she was smiling at him. She had not smiled at him in the water since the Kaiwi Channel in 2013.
"I'm all right," she said. "I've come good."
Her thumb was under the strap.
"Farangis, listen to me."
"No, I have. Honestly. I've come right. It happens about now, doesn't it, you always say it happens about now—"
"Take your hand off the strap."
"What?"
"Take your hand off your shoulder."

She looked at her own hand as if it belonged to a third party. And here is the thing that Dariush Roshanfar will carry: she did not look confused. She looked amused. She looked like a woman who had been caught doing something faintly silly and was about to make a joke about it.
"I'm warm," she said, reasonably.

"You're not warm. You're thirty-three degrees and your shell's opened up and you are about four minutes from being in serious trouble, and I cannot come and get you, and Wilson cannot come and get you, and if anybody puts a hand on you, you are done, so I need you to take your hand off the strap and put your face in the water and swim."
"Dariush—"
"There are four kilometres left."
"I'm hot."

"I know you are," he said. "I know. I know exactly what that is, and I know what it feels like, and I'm telling you it is a lie your skin is telling you, and I am the only person here who can tell you that, and I am three metres away and I am not allowed to touch you, and I have never in my life wanted anything the way I want to come over this rail."
The boat rose and fell.
And Farangis Roshanfar, four kilometres off Scotland, with a core temperature that Dariush would later argue in front of two doctors had been below thirty-three, said:
"Say my name again."
He said her name.
She took her hand off the strap. She put her face in the water. She swam.
At 06:20 Wilson came out of the wheelhouse and stood beside Dariush and neither of them said anything for a while.
"That's them," said Wilson.
"That's what?"
"That's them all. Every one I ever lost." He looked at the water. "They're all lovely at the end. They're all having a great time."
Ailbhe's Log
At 07:00, at hour twenty-nine, with three kilometres to go and the Scottish coast close enough to see the white of the buildings at Portpatrick, Ailbhe Nunan stood up.

She had been sitting under the wheelhouse for twenty-nine hours. She had written eleven pages. She had recorded fifty-eight feeds, forty-one visible jellyfish between midnight and one, a refusal at 04:00, an episode at 06:08, and a stroke rate that had gone from sixty-two to forty-seven.

She walked to the wheelhouse and said something to Wilson, and Wilson looked at her for a moment and then reached up and switched on the hailer, which is a small grey loudspeaker on the wheelhouse roof used for talking to swimmers over an engine and which had not been switched on all night because Dariush's voice carried well enough.
The click of it going live came across the water.
Farangis lifted her head.

And Ailbhe Nunan, fifty-eight years old, twenty-six years an observer, standing on the deck of a boat in the North Channel at seven o'clock in the morning with the Scottish coast three kilometres away, held up a sheet of paper that was ten years old and began to read.
"Observer's log. English Channel Two-Way Attempt. Roshanfar, F. Fifth of September, two thousand and sixteen."
Her voice came out of the grey box flat and administrative and enormous.
"Twenty-three hundred hours. Start. Swimmer clear of water, no assistance."
Dariush turned round very slowly.
"Ailbhe," he said.
She did not stop.
PART FOUR — NUSHDARU
The Omission
She read the whole of it.

Eleven hours of a swim in about six minutes, in the flat official register of the form, over a loudspeaker, to a woman in the water: the start, the water temperatures, the feeds and their durations, the sea state at three-hourly intervals, the turn at the French shore at eleven hours forty, the pace swimmer entering the water at hour eighteen with the time noted and the permission noted and the observer's confirmation that no contact occurred.
And then:
"Zero one forty-two hours. Feed nineteen. Twenty-two seconds. All taken."
"Zero one fifty-one hours. Swimmer stationary."
"Zero two hundred and two hours. Medical emergency on board. Swim abandoned."
The hailer clicked and there was the sound of the engine and nothing else.
Farangis Roshanfar trod water three kilometres off Scotland with her goggles up on her forehead and her lip swollen out and to the left.
"That's it?" she said.
Ailbhe brought the microphone up again.
"That's what's in it."
"Nine minutes."
"Nine minutes."
"There's nine minutes between the feed and the boat turning and you have got two lines in it."
"Yes."
"Where are the eleven seconds."
"They're not in it," said Ailbhe Nunan.

Farangis had known this. That is the thing. She had known it for ten years in the specific way you know the contents of a document you have refused to read: she had constructed the log's contents from Dariush's face in October 2016 when he took an envelope out of a letterbox and read it standing up in a hall and then put it in a drawer. She had known there was nothing in it. She had built the entire architecture of a decade on the certainty that there was nothing in it.
Hearing it was different.
"Say why," she said.
"Farangis, you've three kilometres—"
"Say why!"
And Ailbhe Nunan, who had spent twenty-six years being the person in the boat who has no opinion, put the microphone down for a second and looked at the water, and then picked it up again.

"Because you stopped," she said. "You stopped at zero one fifty-one and the boat turned at zero two hundred and two and I had it on the watch, and it was eleven seconds between you going upright and me saying Marek's name, and I stood on that rail for eleven seconds with a sheet of paper in my hand and I did not know what I was looking at."
The hailer buzzed slightly on the consonants.

"And afterwards I had eleven hours coming back to Dover to write it up. And I knew what would happen to those eleven seconds if I put them in. Because a log is a public document, Farangis. It goes to the association and it goes on a file and every single person in this sport reads them for pleasure, and if I write swimmer stationary eleven seconds prior to alarm then some man in Kent with a website has your son's death and your eleven seconds in the same paragraph by Christmas, and he does the arithmetic, and everybody does the arithmetic, forever."
"So you took it out."
"I put in swimmer stationary and I did not put in the number. That is all I did. I did not falsify a time. The times in that log are correct to the second." She stopped. "I left out an interval."
"You left out the only thing that mattered."
"I left out the thing that would have been used against you by people who were not there."
"You left out my defence," said Farangis Roshanfar.
Nobody on the boat had thought of it that way. It was audible in the deck going quiet.

"For ten years," she said, and her voice was going, not with grief but with the mechanical failure of a throat that had been swallowing salt water for twenty-nine hours, "I have had nothing. Do you understand? I have had no time, no number, no sequence. I have had a hole and my own head, and my own head has been at it every night for ten years, and my own head is not a reliable machine, I found that out at two o'clock this morning. If it had been in the log — if there had been eleven seconds written down by somebody who was not me — I could have gone and looked at it. I could have gone to a piece of paper and read eleven and known it was eleven. Do you know what I've been doing instead?"
Ailbhe said nothing.

"Ninety. Two hundred. Four minutes. Six minutes. I have had nights where it was six minutes, Ailbhe. Where I stood in that water for six minutes and did nothing." She was shaking; even in the water, three kilometres out, they could see it. "You took the only fixed point out of it and you gave me an unlimited one instead, and I have been filling it in for ten years."
"Yes," said Ailbhe Nunan. "I know that now."
"Now."
"I have known it," said Ailbhe, "since about the fourth year."
The Question
"Swim," said Dariush.

She swam. It is one of the more remarkable things about the human animal that she swam. Two and a half kilometres to go, twenty-nine hours in, at a stroke rate of forty-seven, and she put her face in the water and swam, because there was nothing else to do and because she was a person for whom continuing had never required a reason.
At 07:40 the feed went out and she took it without being asked twice.
She gave it back and said, "There's more."
Dariush closed his eyes.
"Ailbhe," said Farangis. "There's more. You didn't come out here at fifty-eight and stand on that rail for twenty-nine hours to tell me about a number."
The hailer clicked.
"No," said Ailbhe Nunan.

The sun was up properly now. Portpatrick was a white line and a green hill behind it and you could see a house with a red roof. There were gannets working about a kilometre to the north. The wind had not come round yet.

"When they got him on the deck," said Ailbhe, "you were still in the water. That's in the log by implication and it's in the log because it has to be — you were not lifted out until zero two hundred and eleven and the swim was abandoned at zero two hundred and two, and I wrote both of those, and both are correct."
"I know."

"And Dariush was doing compressions and Marek was on the radio and the lad had the light on the deck, and I was the only person aboard who did not have a job." She said it evenly. "That's what an observer is at a time like that. A person with no job."
"Ailbhe."

"You were brought aboard at zero two eleven. You had been in the water nineteen hours and twelve minutes and your core, when they got a reading in Dover, was thirty-four point one. You went out on the deck. Not unconscious — down. You were talking. People do talk. It doesn't mean anything and it doesn't get remembered."
Farangis Roshanfar trod water and did not move.

"And I was the one who put a coat over you," said Ailbhe, "because Dariush was busy and there was nobody else, and I knelt down at the top of your head, and your eyes were open, and you were looking straight up at me."
"Ailbhe."
"And you said: does it still count."
The engine ran.
Somewhere off the port bow a gannet went in from thirty metres and came up with nothing.
"That's not true," said Farangis.
"I know."

"That's not — I didn't say that. I asked where he was. That's the first thing I said. I asked where Sohrab was, I've said it a hundred times, I said it to the woman in Belfast, it's the first thing out of my mouth—"
"It was the second thing," said Ailbhe Nunan.
"No."

"About forty seconds later. You asked where he was and I told you they were working on him and you started trying to get up and Dariush shouted at somebody to hold you down." A pause. "That's all true as well. Both are true. You said the first thing and then you said the second thing and I have never in ten years been able to decide which one you meant."
Farangis was going under and coming up. She had stopped treading properly.
"Dariush."
He was at the rail. He had been at the rail for ten minutes.
"Dariush. Did I say it?"

And this is the moment, and everything in the book has been arranged to arrive at it, and it is not a revelation, it is the opposite of a revelation, it is the permanent and irreducible absence of one:
"I didn't hear it," said Dariush Roshanfar.
"That's not what I asked."

"It's what I've got." His voice was perfectly steady and would not be again for three days. "I was doing compressions on my son. I did not hear anything anybody said on that deck, including things I know for a fact were said, including Marek on the radio four feet from my head. I have no memory of the deck at all between about two and two-fifteen. So I did not hear it, and I cannot tell you that you didn't say it, and I have never been able to, and if I told you now that you didn't, you would know I was lying, because you'd know I couldn't know."
"Say it anyway."
"No."
"Dariush. Say it anyway."

"No," he said, "because you'd take it, and it would hold for about a year, and then you'd start asking how I could have known, and you'd end up with two holes instead of one. I'm not doing that to you. Not after last night."

Farangis Roshanfar hung in the water two and a half kilometres off the Scottish coast at hour twenty-nine and forty-five minutes, and understood, completely and finally, the actual shape of the ten years.
She had thought she was carrying a crime.

She was carrying an ambiguity. And an ambiguity does not weigh anything, and does not go anywhere, and cannot be paid off, and admits of no sentence, and is not the kind of thing a human being is built to carry, and she had been carrying one for a decade, and had been dressing it as a crime every single night because a crime is a shape and this had no shape at all.

And every act of mourning she had performed in ten years — every early morning, every eighty-kilometre week, every one of the four times she had stood in front of a drawer, this channel, this swim, this thirty hours, the whole edifice — had been, she saw now, an argument. Directed at nobody. Submitted to no court. A ten-year attempt to demonstrate, by conduct, to an absent authority, that she was the kind of woman who would have asked about her son first.

You cannot prove that. There is no evidence that would settle it. And the only person who could have told her what he saw when he looked across at her, at hour nineteen, in the dark, was not available for comment.
"Swim," said Dariush.
She swam.
Nushdaru
Two kilometres.

The last two kilometres of a channel are the longest object in the sport, because the coast is now visible in detail — she could see cars — and the mind, which has spent thirty hours in a room thirty minutes wide, breaks out of the room and looks at the whole distance at once and says: that is nothing, that is twenty minutes, that is a warm-up.
It was not twenty minutes. At forty-seven strokes a minute against the last of the ebb it was an hour and forty.

And somewhere in it, in the last of it, with the presence still swimming on her left where it had been for nine hours, Farangis Roshanfar told herself the story. Not deliberately. It came the way the kitchen smell had come, and the orchestra, and the orange cap: unbidden, complete, in her mother's voice, in Persian, which she had not been able to read at speed since she was fourteen and could still hear perfectly.
It is the oldest story her people have and it is about a father and a son and about how long it takes for help to arrive.

There is a champion. He is the greatest of them, the one every country invents and then spends a thousand years being embarrassed by: enormous, ungovernable, contemptuous of kings, the only man who can be sent when a thing is genuinely lost. Rostam.
And travelling, years before, he fathers a child in a border town on a woman he stays with for one night, and he leaves her an armlet, and he goes, and he does not come back, and he does not ask.

The child is a boy. He grows very fast — the story is insistent on this, that he is a man at ten — and he grows up knowing exactly who his father is, and the whole of his short life is organised around one intention, which is to find him. Not to fight him. To find him. He raises an army for it. He goes to war for it, on the wrong side, for the sole purpose of turning over enough of the world that his father is obliged to come out of it.

And the mother, who knows what is coming, does the only thing available to her, which is to say nothing. She does not send word. She is afraid of what the champion will do and she is afraid of losing the boy, and she keeps the two of them apart with silence, and the silence works, right up until it doesn't.
They meet at a river.

They do not know each other. That is the whole engine of it and there is nothing supernatural in the mechanism: the boy has never seen his father's face, and the father has been told by everyone that the enemy champion is somebody else, and he is old, and he is arrogant, and he does not ask a young man's name before a duel because a young man's name is not worth the delay.

The boy asks. Twice. Three times. He asks directly — are you Rostam — because he has heard something in the man's voice or seen something in the way he stands, and every time he asks, the father lies. Out of caution. Out of tactics. Because a champion does not give his name to an unknown challenger, because it is a rule, because it is what you do.
They fight for two days.

On the first day the boy has him. He has him down and his knee is on him and the knife is out, and the father, who is finished, says: it is not our custom to kill a man on the first fall; the custom is to let him up, and to kill him on the second.
There is no such custom.
The boy, who is seventeen and has been raised on courtesy and has no reason on earth to doubt the greatest warrior alive on a point of etiquette, lets him up.
The second day the father wins.

And he puts the knife in, into the side, under the ribs, and the boy goes down, and while he is dying he says the thing that everyone who hears this story at seven years old carries for the rest of their life. He says: this is nothing. I did this to myself. But my father will come. He will hear that a boy was killed at this river and he will come and find you, and there is nowhere on the earth you can go.
And the father says: what father.
And the boy tells him, and undoes the armour at the shoulder, and there is an armlet.
Now. Here is the part that is actually the story, and it is not the killing, because the killing is only the setup.
The boy is not dead.

He is dying, but not dead, not for some hours yet, and the father knows exactly what will save him. There is a medicine. The king has it — the vain, contemptible, small-minded king who has been afraid of Rostam for thirty years and has been waiting all that time for one single occasion on which the great man would have to ask him for something.
Nushdaru. The remedy. It is in a chest in the king's tent, half a day away.
And Rostam sends a rider.

And the king reads the message and puts it down and thinks about it. He thinks about what Rostam will become if the boy lives. He thinks about the two of them together. He thinks — and the poet gives him this thought, and it is the most contemporary sentence in the whole of the epic — about his own position.
And he does not say no.
He delays.

He asks the messenger to wait. He requires the great man to come himself. He extends the hour, and the hour, and the afternoon, and it costs him nothing, and it is entirely deniable, and at no point does he refuse.
Rostam rides for it himself in the end.
And the poet — and this is why the thing has lasted a thousand years — does not have him fail on the road, or be intercepted, or lose the way.
He has him arrive.
He is on the road with the remedy in his hand when the messenger comes the other way to tell him that his son died an hour ago.

The medicine existed. It was real. It worked. It was in a chest, half a day away, and it was on its way, and it was in the correct hands, and it was travelling as fast as a horse can travel, and none of that mattered, because the only thing that has ever mattered in the entire history of any of this is whether the help arrives before the hour.
Farangis Roshanfar swam the last two kilometres of the North Channel with that in her, in her mother's voice.

Four minutes. That is what it took, that night, from the boat turning to her son on the deck: eleven seconds to the screw, ninety seconds to the boat coming round and Dariush over the side, the rest to get him up. Four minutes, in the dark, in a swell, over the side of a moving vessel, by a crew of four with one of them a boy.
She had done the arithmetic ten thousand times and had always run it as an accusation. Four minutes. Four minutes in which she did nothing.

And she saw now, in the last kilometre, with the town coming up, what the story had been telling her since she was seven years old and what she had heard every single time without once understanding it:
Four minutes was fast.

Four minutes was a competent crew doing the correct things in the correct order at three in the morning in the English Channel, and it was faster than almost anybody would have managed, and her husband was in the water inside a hundred seconds, and the compressions were textbook and were begun inside four minutes and were given by a consultant anaesthetist, which is the single best set of hands that could possibly have been on that deck.
And a nineteen-year-old boy died anyway.
There was no king. Nobody delayed. Nobody was afraid of anybody's position. The rider went at once and rode as hard as a horse can be ridden and the remedy was real and it arrived.
And the hour had already passed.

That is the story. That has always been the story. It is not a story about blame; that is what children take from it, and what she had taken from it for forty years. It is a story about the fact that the world contains intervals which are shorter than any possible response, and that inside those intervals there is no such thing as culpability, and that human beings would rather have a villain — a vain king, a lying father, a mother's silence, a woman who stopped swimming for eleven seconds — than accept that a thing can simply be too fast.
She was four hundred metres off the Scottish shore.
She turned her head to the left, at the top of a breath, into the empty water where a presence had been swimming beside her since twenty past one in the morning.
There was nobody there.
There had been nobody there since twenty past one in the morning.
She put her face down and swam.
Shingle
The last four hundred metres of a channel swim are done in water that has a bottom in it, and the bottom is the strangest thing a marathon swimmer ever sees.

For thirty hours there has been nothing underneath. Not darkness — absence; a volume of water going down two hundred metres to a floor that has no relationship to the swimmer whatsoever. And then, at some point in the last few hundred metres, the light comes back off something, and there is kelp, brown and moving, four metres down, and then rock, and then, at about a metre and a half, stones.
Swimmers weep at this. Grown men, world-ranked, weep at the kelp.

Portpatrick has a small harbour with two piers and a shingle beach to the north of it that the swims come into on the flood. There were people on the pier, because there are always people on the pier: eleven or twelve of them at twenty to ten on a Saturday morning in August, some of them because they had heard, most of them because there was a boat coming in close and a thing happening.

Wilson brought the Kestrel Star round to seaward and held her at forty metres and killed the way off her, because the boat cannot follow into the shallows and because the final approach is the one part of the entire crossing that the swimmer does alone in the sense that people imagine the whole thing is done alone.
Ailbhe Nunan came to the rail with the watch.

The rule for the finish is precise, and it is the last cruelty, and every marathon swimmer knows it before they ever get in: the swim is complete when the swimmer clears the water under her own power, on dry land, without assistance, upright.
Not when she touches. Not when she stands. She must get out.

And she must do it after thirty-one hours in twelve-degree water, with a core temperature around thirty-three, on legs that have not borne weight since the day before yesterday and have had no meaningful blood in them for a day, over wet shingle, in a swell, alone, while eleven people watch from a pier and a boat holds at forty metres with her husband on it.

People have failed here. Not many, but enough that everyone knows the names. There is a man who got to the stones in Wissant and could not get up, four times, and was taken out by his crew at the fifth attempt, and whose swim does not exist.
Farangis Roshanfar came into the shallows at 09:38.
She got her feet down at 09:39 and could not stand, and went over sideways into eighteen inches of water, and got up onto her hands and knees.
On the boat, nobody said anything.

She crawled about four metres on her hands and knees through the wash, with the swell coming in behind her and pushing her forward and then dragging back, and the stones under her palms, and her hands did not feel the stones at all.
At the tide line she stopped.
Thirty-one hours and thirty-eight minutes.

She knelt on wet shingle on the Scottish coast with her head down and the water running off her and the whole of her back and shoulders and forearms and face swollen in long red weals in a pattern nobody would ever be able to read, and she put both hands flat on the stones.
Then she got one foot under her.
Then the other.

Then she stood up, on a beach at Portpatrick, at 09:40 in the morning, out of the water, upright, under her own power, unassisted, and eleven people on a pier who had no idea what they were looking at made a small ragged noise, and Ailbhe Nunan pressed a watch and wrote a time on a sheet of paper.
"Nine forty," she said. "Thirty-one hours, forty minutes. Swimmer clear."
Wilson put a hand on the horn and left it there for four seconds.
And Farangis Roshanfar stood on the stones with her arms hanging and her mouth open and looked at the place where nobody was standing.
That is the part that does not go into the log.

There is a shape that lives at the end of every swim she has ever done since she was thirty-seven, and the shape is a young man on a beach with a coat over his arm and both hands held up with the fingers spread, and it is not there, and the not-being-there of it is a physical object with edges, and she stood on the shingle at Portpatrick and looked directly at it for eleven seconds.
Then Dariush came off the boat.

He came in the tender with Ryan rowing and he was over the side in a metre of water in his shoes and he came up the shingle at a speed that a man of fifty-two should not attempt on wet stones, and about two metres away he stopped, hard, because thirty-one hours of the rule does not switch off in a man's body just because a watch has been pressed.
He stopped, and he looked at Ailbhe.
And Ailbhe Nunan, standing in the bow of a small boat with a clipboard, said: "It's done. Go on."
He put his coat around her.

That was all it was. He put a coat around his wife's shoulders on a beach in Wigtownshire and then he put his arms round her on top of it, and the first human contact Farangis Roshanfar had had in thirty-one hours and forty minutes was the weight of a man's hands flat between her shoulder blades, and she made a sound that the eleven people on the pier heard and did not understand and went home and did not talk about.
She said, into his shoulder, through a mouth that would not work: "Four minutes."
"What?"
"Four minutes," she said. "That's fast."
And Dariush Roshanfar, who had been waiting ten years for a sentence and had long ago stopped expecting one, held onto his wife on a beach and said, "Yes. It was fast."
The Signature

They took her to the hotel on the front because it was closer than the hospital and because the correct treatment for a swimmer at thirty-three degrees is not a hospital, it is dry clothes, a room at twenty-two degrees, blankets, warm sweet drinks, and time — and above all it is slowly, because a rapid rewarming drives the shell open again and drops the core further, which is the mistake everyone's instinct makes and which kills people in the hour after rescue rather than in the water.

She was shaking so hard at eleven o'clock that she could not hold a cup. That is normal and is in fact a good sign; the shivering is thermogenesis and a person who has stopped shivering is in a different category. By half past one she had stopped shaking. By three she had eaten a bowl of soup and most of a bread roll and had fallen asleep sitting up with the roll in her hand.

At half past four in the afternoon she came downstairs into the residents' lounge in borrowed clothes, with her lower lip still out and to the left and her forearms in long raised weals going from red to purple, and her hands, which would not have full sensation for eleven days.
Ailbhe Nunan was at a table by the window with the log.

Eleven pages, plus the observer's declaration on the last one. The declaration is a short paragraph in a small font which states that the observer witnessed the swim, that it was conducted in accordance with the rules, that no assistance was given and no contact occurred, and that the times and conditions recorded are true to the best of the observer's knowledge.
She had signed it. Her signature was at the bottom, in blue, with the date.
Under it there was a second line, and the second line was empty, and beside the empty line there was a pen.
"You'll want to read it," said Ailbhe.
Farangis sat down. It took her some time.
She read the eleven pages. It took her about twenty minutes and nobody said anything while she did it. Dariush stood at the window with his back to the room.

The log recorded, in a small neat hand, a swim of thirty-one hours and forty minutes across the North Channel from Donaghadee to Portpatrick, in water between eleven point nine and twelve point four degrees, in a costume conforming to the rules, without contact or assistance of any kind. It recorded fifty-eight feeds. It recorded extensive envenomation from midnight onward. It recorded a refusal at 04:00 and its resolution. It recorded an episode at 06:08 in the observer's own words: swimmer became disoriented and attempted to remove costume strap; feeder addressed her verbally; swimmer resumed.
And in the second column, at 07:00, it recorded:

Observer read aloud, at swimmer's request made at hour ten and repeated at hour twenty-nine, the observer's log of the swimmer's English Channel two-way attempt of 5 September 2016, in which this observer served as junior observer. Observer confirmed to the swimmer that an interval of eleven seconds between the swimmer becoming stationary and the alarm being raised was omitted from that log by this observer's decision. Observer further disclosed a statement made by the swimmer on the deck of the pilot vessel following recovery, which was not recorded at the time and is not corroborated. This disclosure is entered here at the observer's own initiative.
It was the longest observer's remark in the eleven pages.
"You put it in," said Farangis.
"I did."
"You didn't have to."
"No."
"It'll go to the association. It'll be on a file. Some man in Kent with a website—"
"Yes," said Ailbhe Nunan.
Farangis Roshanfar looked at it for a long time.
"Why now?"

"Because I did it the other way once," said Ailbhe, "and I thought I was being kind, and I watched what it did to you for ten years, and I am fifty-eight, and I would like at some point before I stop doing this to have written down a true thing that cost me something."
She pushed the pen about an inch across the table.

"That's the swimmer's declaration. You sign, it goes to the association, they ratify. You'd be the hundred and twenty-seventh person to cross the North Channel and the eighth woman over forty-five, and there's people who'd want to talk to you about it."
Farangis put her hand flat beside the pen. The fingers still did not close.
Here is what a signature is.
It is not a receipt. It is a statement, by the swimmer, that the log is a true account of what happened in the water.
That is all it has ever been and that is why the sport rests on it.
And she had, that morning, at hour twenty-four, in the middle of the North Channel, in the dark, watched her own memory calmly and confidently change the colour of her son's cap.

Everything in those eleven pages was true. She did not doubt one word of it. The times were right. The temperatures were right. Ailbhe Nunan had spent thirty-one hours writing down exactly what she saw and had then gone further than she had to.
But the document did not say this is what the observer saw. It said, on the second line, in the swimmer's own hand: I confirm this is a true account.

And Farangis Roshanfar was no longer a person who could put her name to a sentence like that. Not about that night, and not about this one, and not about the ten years in between, and not about anything that had happened inside her own head, which she now knew to be an instrument that rebuilds the room every time you open the door.

She had come out here to be charged with something. She had spent ten years and about forty thousand pounds and a marriage's worth of silence assembling a court, and she had got, at hour twenty-nine, the only verdict that was ever available, which was that there is no verdict, that the interval was shorter than any possible response, that the remedy was on the road and the hour had passed, and that the last person on earth who could have told her what he saw was nineteen and is not available.
There is nothing to sign.
"No," she said.
Ailbhe Nunan did not move.
"You did it," she said. "I watched you do it. Thirty-one hours and forty minutes. It happened."
"I know it happened."
"If you don't sign, it doesn't exist. There's no ratification. There's no name on the list. It's a boat trip."
"I know."
"Farangis."
"It happened," said Farangis Roshanfar, "and I'm not going to certify it."
Dariush turned round from the window.

And there is a moment in which he could have said something, and he had, over ten years, several thousand things prepared, and he looked at his wife sitting in borrowed clothes in a residents' lounge in Portpatrick with her hands ruined and her mouth ruined and the pen an inch from her fingers, and he did not say any of them.
He said: "Are you cold?"
"Yes."
"Right," he said, and took his coat off the back of the chair, and put it around her shoulders.
Ailbhe Nunan closed the log.

She put it in the canvas bag with the thermometer and the watch, and she stood up, and she put her hand on the back of the chair for a second on the way past — not on Farangis, on the chair — and she said, "I'll be in Sligo. You have the number."

And she went out through the lounge and out onto the front, where the boats were, and the tide was going, and the whole grey-green channel lay out to the west with thirty-four and a half kilometres of nothing in it and Ireland on the far side, entirely invisible, exactly where it had been the whole time.
